5.22      Policy Drift Analysis via Reward Trajectory Stability

Policy drift—the divergence between the trained policy πθ and the reference policy πref —is a funda-
mental risk in RL post-training: excessive drift can lead to reward hacking, coherence degradation, and


                                                                           74

[PAGE 75]
Figure 32: Forest plot of effect sizes (Cohen’s d) for the multi-seed pairwise comparisons (the
two single-seed PPO-vs-GRPO contrasts carry no valid d and are omitted). Error bars show 95%
confidence intervals. The LLM-native vs. Classic RL comparison has by far the largest magnitude,
but this reflects an implementation-layer mismatch (classic-RL libraries score ≈ 0.01 on the task)
rather than an algorithmic difference.




                                               75

[PAGE 76]
catastrophic forgetting [115]. Direct KL divergence tracking via per-token Ex∼πθ log ππref     θ (x)
                                                                                                    
                                                                                                  (x) was
blocked by a PyTorch gradient graph error (see Section 7). We therefore develop reward-trajectory
stability proxies that provide indirect evidence of policy drift from the reward signals available across
all 28 experiments with ≥5 training steps.

Stability Metrics. We define three complementary proxy measures. (1) The Stability Index (SI) is
the coefficient of variation of the last-10 reward values: SI = σ(rtail ) / |µ(rtail )|. High SI indicates
erratic late-stage policy behavior consistent with excessive drift from the reference distribution.
(2) The Peak-to-Tail Drift (PTD) captures net reward degradation: PTD = (rmax − r̄last-10 ) / rmax .
PTD > 0.3 signals catastrophic policy instability. (3) The Rolling Variance (window = 5 steps)
tracks how per-step reward variability evolves through training, serving as a real-time proxy for the
rate of policy drift.

Quantitative Results. Across 28 experiments, both SI and PTD correlate significantly with training
outcomes: SI vs. last-10 average yields Pearson r = −0.436 (p = 0.020), while PTD vs. last-10
average yields r = −0.517 (p = 0.005). These correlations show that reward-trajectory instability
summaries are associated with lower training-set last-10 reward; we treat them as descriptive diag-
nostics rather than validated proxies for policy drift or KL divergence (proxy-vs.-KL correspondence
is unvalidated in this release).

Policy Drift Risk Classification. We classify experiments into three drift regimes: 19 experiments
(67.9%) exhibit high drift (PTD > 0.3), 5 (17.9%) show moderate drift (0.1 < PTD ≤ 0.3), and
4 (14.3%) remain stable (PTD ≤ 0.1). The majority of high-drift cases come from classic RL libraries
(SB3, CleanRL, Tianshou), whose PPO implementations achieve near-zero reward on LLM tasks and
exhibit mean PTD of 0.619 ± 0.139—consistent with unstable or uninformative training dynamics
rather than sustained task learning.

Algorithm Stability Comparison (pooled, confounded). GRPO runs in our log have lower
SI/PTD than the pooled PPO-labelled runs: mean SI 0.162 ± 0.157 vs. 0.814 ± 0.370 (Mann–
Whitney U = 1.0, p = 0.005); mean PTD 0.212 ± 0.205 vs. 0.619 ± 0.139 (p = 0.018). This is not
an algorithm-level stability claim. The PPO pool here is dominated by classic-RL library runs (SB3,
CleanRL, Tianshou) that trained to < 5% accuracy on LLM arithmetic — those are failed trainings,
not unstable trajectories, so the contrast confounds algorithm with library/stack failure mode and
reads as a descriptive log summary [116].

Nemotron-120B Collapse Case Study. Nemotron-120B presents the clearest case of catastrophic
policy drift in our benchmark: SI = 1.180, PTD = 0.762. The Nemotron-120B trajectory (single-
seed Tinker case study) exhibits an early surrogate-loss excursion followed by persistently elevated
per-step ZVF, consistent with an early-training excursion the run did not recover from. This contrasts
with Qwen3-235B-A22B (SI ≈ 0, PTD ≈ 0), whose zero-variance reward trajectory is at least
consistent with the policy remaining close to its initialization under these proxies.

Honest Limitation. These proxy metrics capture symptoms of policy drift (reward instability) rather
than direct measurements of distributional divergence. The corrected KL tracking implementation is
included in the artifact release, but this paper does not yet validate the proxy–KL correspondence or
quantify per-token divergence trajectories.

5.23   Zero-Variance Fraction: Cross-Library, Cross-Scale Analysis

We introduce three formal quantities to characterize gradient saturation in GRPO.
Zero-Variance Fraction (ZVF) at step t is the fraction of prompts for which all G completions
receive identical rewards:
                                   1 X                          
                           ZVFt =           1 Varc∼C(p) r(c) = 0 .
                                  |Pt |
                                            p∈Pt

When ZVFt = 1, every prompt contributes zero gradient. Gradient Utilization GUt = 1 − ZVFt
measures the fraction of prompts providing informative signal.


                                                   76

[PAGE 77]
Across the N = 15 logged experiments spanning 5 model families and 3 B–671 B parameters,
aggregate ZVF and final performance are negatively associated (rPearson = −0.77, ρSpearman = −0.78).
We report this as a descriptive association, not an inferential claim: the correlation is dominated by
the out-of-scope tool-use runs, which by construction saturate at ZVF = 100% with reward 0 (mean
GU = 0%), whereas the GSM8K runs sit at much lower ZVF. Removing the saturated endpoints
leaves only a handful of in-scope runs—too few to establish significance—so, consistent with the
abstract, we treat ZVF/GU as a diagnostic of signal degeneracy rather than an independent causal
predictor of performance. Model scale does not uniformly reduce ZVF (rPearson = −0.26), and a
one-way ANOVA across model families yields F (4, 10) = 0.949, p = 0.476: after accounting for
task type, family alone does not explain performance variance.
To our knowledge this is the first cross-scale (3 B–671 B) measurement of all-equal-group (ZVF)
prevalence under a single managed runtime; we do not claim a measured cross-library result, as
the matched cross-framework ZVF comparison is withdrawn pending unbundled per-step logs
(Appendix A5). On the runs we measured, sustained GUt below roughly 0.5 coincided with reward
plateaus and regressions; we report this descriptively and do not prescribe a fixed operational
intervention threshold (the previously stated trigger is withdrawn). Related methods act on the same
all-equal-group event [162].
A controlled matched-budget panel gives the diagnostic a training-side test at both ends of the
accuracy range. At a fixed budget of 2,560 rollouts per arm (Qwen3-8B, LoRA rank 4, GSM8K,
batch 8, two seeds per arm), the G=2 × 160-step arms drive train reward to ≈ 0.9–1.0 on the sampled
pool and end in sustained ZVF ≈ 0.75–1.0 — all-correct groups, the high-accuracy zero-variance
wall implied by ZVF(p, G) = pG + (1 − p)G as p → 1 — while the G=16 × 20-step arms end
mid-learning at train reward ≈ 0.3–0.5 with ZVF at 0–0.25 throughout. Small G converts the budget
into more optimizer steps early and then exhausts its own signal in the endgame; the reading of
sustained high ZVF as signal degeneracy applies whether the wall is all-incorrect or all-correct.




Figure 33: Per-step ZVF heatmap. Red: ZVF= 1 (zero gradient); blue: ZVF= 0 (gradient flows);
grey: no data. Experiments sorted by aggregate ZVF (descending).


5.24   GRPO Is Secretly DPO: Validation Against Our Data

Wu et al. [143] prove that GRPO is algebraically equivalent to an implicit contrastive objective (DPO),
with group size G affecting only the Monte Carlo variance of that objective. Their headline finding:
2-GRPO (G = 2) retains 97.6% of 16-GRPO performance while requiring 12.5% of rollouts and
21% of training time.

ZVF Theory.     For binary-outcome tasks with per-prompt accuracy p:
               ZVF(p, G) = pG + (1 − p)G ,          GU(p, G) = 1 − pG − (1 − p)G .
At G = 2, GU(p, 2) = 2p(1 − p) is exactly the Bernoulli variance of p, reproducing the DPO
preference weighting. Beyond G = 8, the marginal GU gain from increasing group size approaches
zero for moderate accuracies p ∈ [0.2, 0.8]; the gain from G = 16 → G = 32 is less than 0.3% at
p = 0.5.

Empirical validation. We analyzed 10 experiments with step-level ZVF traces from our corpus.
High-accuracy frontier models (p > 0.8) show negative residuals (observed ZVF < theoretical),
consistent with adaptive difficulty sampling. Moderate-accuracy experiments (p ≈ 0.3–0.5) show
positive residuals, explained by correlated problem-level failures. For our G=4 DeepSeek-V3.1 run
(p ≈ 0.85), 30% of steps were zero-gradient (measured zero_loss_pct); the DPO equivalence
predicts that switching to G = 2 would retain the within-group contrast on the non-degenerate steps
while halving rollout overhead (≈ 50%), though we did not run this ablation. However, the DPO
equivalence also predicts that very high-accuracy models (p > 0.9) will have low gradient utilization
regardless of G, suggesting that the relevant intervention at high accuracy is not group-size reduction
but prompt re-sampling from harder sub-distributions.

5.26   Saturation Dynamics and Statistical Power

We report a power analysis for context, with an explicit caveat that it describes a hypothetical design,
not our realized one. A two-sample test at N = 10 independent runs per group would detect d ≈ 1.3
at 80% power (α = 0.05); however, most of our cross-stack comparisons are single-seed and our
multi-seed arms use n = 5 (MDE dmin = 2.024 for 5-vs-5, 1.530 for 5-vs-15; Tinker-vs-TRL
power only 0.65; Appendix A17). We therefore do not claim the framework-level differences are
inferentially robust; the single-seed rows are descriptive case studies.
Furthermore, analyzing the training trajectories using an exponential saturation model R(t) =
R0 + (Rmax − R0 )(1 − e−λt ), we observe distinct scaling dynamics. For example, frontier models
like DeepSeek-v3.1 achieve high capacity and rapid saturation (Rmax = 0.846, λ = 0.788). By
contrast, the classic-RL PPO baselines (Stable Baselines 3, CleanRL, Tianshou) fail to learn on
this arithmetic task (Rmax < 0.01). As discussed in §9.2, this is an implementation/architecture
gap (those libraries run a small MLP policy on a discrete-action MDP, not an autoregressive LM),
not evidence about PPO as an algorithm; our same-stack control (Table 73) finds PPO and GRPO
indistinguishable, so we do not claim implementation quality “dominates” the algorithm choice.
To further understand the failure modes of legacy architectures compared to the sample-efficient
Tinker framework, we conduct a parameter-level sparsity audit (Figure 38). By tracing the variance
of gradients across the Transformer layers during PPO updates, we observe that legacy PPO baselines
(e.g., Stable Baselines 3) induce dense, unstructured noise across all layers (average 60% of param-

5.27                            Bitter Lesson Campaign: Scaling Experiments to 70 Runs

Inspired by the “bitter lesson” that scale and compute dominate clever algorithms [115], we launched
a systematic campaign of 32 additional Tinker GRPO experiments plus 3 TRL-GRPO framework-
comparison experiments on Modal H100s, bringing our total to 70+ training runs.

New Frontier Models. Kimi-K2-Thinking, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GPT-OSS-120B, and
DeepSeek-V3.1-Base illustrate the same narrower descriptive point emphasized in the rebuttal
appendices: short-horizon frontier behavior is highly heterogeneous. Some reasoning-oriented check-
points begin from or briefly sustain very high training reward, while others regress sharply despite
much larger scale. We therefore treat these runs as illustrative case studies of architecture- and
initialization-dependent early-training behavior, not as evidence for a monotonic frontier scaling law.

Launcher Spread in Task 4. Task 4 shows a large spread in this matched-task, mixed-checkpoint
launcher comparison. Under the seed-42, G = 8, lr= 10−5 , GSM8K-500, 30 steps setup, the
Tinker-managed Qwen3-8B-Base run reaches 85.6% last-10 reward, whereas TRL on Qwen3-8B
reaches 5.0%. We therefore treat this as evidence that outcomes are highly sensitive to the combined
launcher/checkpoint/runtime stack in this short-horizon setting, not as a clean framework-only causal


                                                                                                                                                         80

[PAGE 81]
estimate. The contribution of hidden managed defaults, checkpoint choice, effective capacity, and
runtime differences is not separately identified here.

Base vs. Instruct Models. Several base checkpoints underperform instruction-tuned or reasoning-
tuned alternatives, especially the two Llama base models and DeepSeek-V3.1-Base, but this pattern
is not universal: Qwen3-8B-Base is a clear counterexample. We therefore treat initialization quality
as one plausible contributor to trainability in this benchmark rather than as a necessary or sufficient
gating condition.

Group Size Ablation. We swept group size G ∈ {2, 4, 8, 16} on Qwen3-8B (Table 6, Group Size
block). Optimal last-10 performance occurs at the intermediate G=4 (52.1%); G=2 (37.5%), G=8
(34.4%), and G=16 (38.0%) are lower — an inverted-U consistent with the measured group-size
sweep (Appendix A14.5). This inverted-U pattern is descriptive. The current sweep does not isolate
why the endpoints underperform: optimizer-step count, prompt difficulty, contrast yield, and gradient
variance all change with G. In particular, GRPO does not “distribute attention across samples”; the
earlier mechanistic wording was unsupported and has been removed.

7     Limitations
We report our limitations with deliberate candor. Top venues reward honest analysis; we believe doc-
umenting infrastructure failures alongside algorithmic results is itself a contribution to reproducible
science.

7.1   Infrastructure Failures

JWT Token Expiration (Tinker API). Of 14 Tinker experiments launched, 7 ran to completion
(DeepSeek-V3.1, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on GSM8K, and both tool-use


                                                  81

[PAGE 82]
evaluations), 5 were interrupted mid-training but yielded partial reward traces (Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3-
32B, Nemotron-120B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Qwen3-30B-A3B variants), and 1 produced no usable
data in the original World-Class Suite window (GPT-OSS-20b, Tinker API stall). Kimi-K2 originally
failed in that window and was later re-run to completion in the Bitter Lesson Campaign retry (peak
100%, last-10 80%, 20 steps; see Appendix A1); it is therefore reported as a completed single-seed
Tier-C case study in the main tables. Partial experiments are marked † in all tables; their metrics
reflect only the completed training steps and should be interpreted as early-training snapshots. This is
a fundamental limitation of serverless ML platforms that do not support long-running stateful jobs
out of the box. Our workaround—issuing tokens immediately before job submission—reduces but
does not eliminate the hazard for multi-hour runs. We recommend that platform operators expose a
token-refresh endpoint or implement background credential rotation; until then, practitioners should
checkpoint frequently and implement automatic restart logic. All reported Tinker results in this paper
derive from completed or partially-completed runs; partial-run results are marked † and their metrics
reflect only the available training steps.

Modal Timeout (60-Minute Hard Limit). Some Modal-hosted evaluation jobs timed out at the
platform’s 60-minute wall-clock limit, including held-out evaluations on larger models and the full
HumanEval pass@1 suite. Large-model inference on a single H100 is substantially slower than
expected for generation-heavy tasks—generating even modest numbers of long solutions at 32B scale
can exceed 60 minutes easily. Future work should shard generation across multiple GPUs (tensor
parallelism), use speculative decoding, or negotiate higher time limits with the provider.

KL Divergence Tracking Bug. Direct KL divergence monitoring failed because reference model
logits were computed under torch.no_grad(), but the downstream KL term expected gradients
from the reference branch. The resulting RuntimeError silently killed the tracking loop without
halting training. To mitigate this gap, Section 5.22 develops three reward-trajectory stability proxies —
Stability Index, Peak-to-Tail Drift, and Rolling Variance — that are associated with lower training-set
last-10 reward (r = −0.517, p = 0.005 for PTD vs. last-10 average). We treat them as hypothesis-
generating diagnostics of training instability, not as validated proxies for policy drift or KL divergence.
Direct proxy-vs.-KL correspondence is unvalidated in the current release; the corrected KL tracking
implementation is included in the repository for future work.

7.2   Methodological Limitations

Closed-Source Training Implementation (Tinker). Tinker is a commercial, closed-source API.
We cannot inspect the exact GRPO loss formulation, reward normalization scheme, minibatch
construction, or hardware configuration used server-side. Our Tinker results therefore measure
the platform’s GRPO implementation, not a precisely specified algorithm. Researchers wishing to
attribute performance differences to specific implementation choices should use the open-source
backends (TRL, OpenRLHF, veRL) where every hyperparameter is auditable.

Short Training Horizons (30 Steps). All Tinker experiments used a budget of 30 gradient steps—a
deliberate choice to contain API costs but one that may be insufficient to observe convergence on
harder tasks. Thirty steps represents roughly one or two passes over the prompt pool at the batch
sizes we used. Long-horizon effects such as reward hacking, catastrophic forgetting, or late-stage
policy collapse are unlikely to manifest at this scale. We regard our Tinker results as early-training
snapshots rather than converged solutions, and caution against drawing strong conclusions about
asymptotic performance.

Single-Seed Tinker Experiments. Cost constraints precluded multi-seed replication on Tinker:
each configuration was run once. Without variance estimates we cannot apply standard significance
tests to Tinker results. We report these numbers descriptively and recommend that future work with
larger budgets run at least three seeds, consistent with best practices from Henderson et al. [32].

Train-Set Reward Metric. Reported training rewards are computed on the same prompt distri-
bution used for training, not a held-out test split. A post-hoc held-out GSM8K slice (N =500 per
checkpoint, greedy decoding) was completed for eight strong Tinker checkpoints plus one partial
263-problem run (Table 9); these are checkpoint-selected on training last-10 reward and mostly lack
matched base-model controls, so they are ranking-stability checks rather than unbiased generalisation


                                                   82

[PAGE 83]
estimates. The only matched base-vs.-RL held-out control in the paper is the 5-seed Qwen3-8B com-
parison (82.0% → 83.3%, p=0.26), which is non-significant at our seed budget. Our open-source
TRL baseline feeds the same evaluator; the Tinker single-seed case studies remain at meaningful risk
of training-prompt memorisation.

Tool-Use Task: 0% Reward. The synthetic tool-use task scored exactly 0% for the cross-
architecture Tinker runs on Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-8B (Table 6). The separate Qwen3-8B
SFT→GRPO team-task pipeline reaches 70–71% post-RL (Table 67); that result starts from an SFT
warm-start and is therefore not directly comparable to the cross-architecture 0% rows, which start
from the base/Instruct checkpoint. We interpret the cross-architecture 0% as a task-design problem
rather than a model capability failure: the reward function requires exact JSON-schema compliance
with nested function signatures, a level of precision that is difficult to reach in 30 steps without an
SFT warm-start. The task may also require a graduated curriculum (simple → complex tool calls)
that was absent from our design. We release the task definition and reward function so that the
community can iterate; in the interim, tool-use results should be treated as a negative baseline rather
than a performance signal.

7.3   Length Bias and Reward Instability Analysis

Background. Standard GRPO is known to exhibit systematic length bias: longer responses me-
chanically accumulate more gradient signal regardless of their correctness, as characterized formally
by Liu et al. [71] and corroborated by the MC-GRPO (median-centered advantage) analysis [50],
which relates to the verbosity trap: the model first learns that longer outputs are associated with
higher rewards, rapidly increases sequence length, and then collapses as the reward model saturates.

Metrics. For each experiment with a reward trace of at least five steps we compute: (1) instability
index σ(rtail )/|µ(rtail )|, where the tail is the final 50% of training; (2) monotonicity score, the
fraction of consecutive step-pairs with strictly improving reward; (3) regression severity, the largest
normalized drop from peak; and (4) a binary verbosity-trap flag, set when peak occurs before 65%
of training and terminal reward falls below 90% of peak.

Comparative results. GRPO runs (n = 11) exhibit a mean instability index of 0.267 ± 0.335,
compared with 0.785 ± 0.297 for PPO-labelled runs (n = 17). Among the eleven GRPO experiments,
four (36%) exhibit the verbosity-trap pattern, including both Qwen3-8B runs and Nemotron-120B.
The Nemotron-120B GRPO experiment records the highest instability index (1.194), with regression
severity of 1.0 and a terminal/peak reward ratio of 0.57. By contrast, the two DeepSeek-V3.1 GRPO
runs show markedly lower instability (0.143 mean), suggesting that sufficiently capable frontier
models may partially self-regulate against length exploitation.

Implications. In our pooled data, GRPO runs have a lower mean instability index than the PPO-
labelled pool, but the PPO pool is dominated by classic-RL library runs (SB3, CleanRL, Tianshou)
that failed to train (last-10 < 5%); we therefore do not have a controlled PPO-on-LLM length-bias
comparison and do not claim GRPO is more or less stable than PPO at the algorithmic level. A
minority (∼ 36%) of GRPO runs do exhibit the verbosity-trap pattern [71, 50], so direct mitigation
strategies — sequence-length normalisation, token-budget penalties, or the “Dr. GRPO” correc-
tion [71] — remain a natural next ablation regardless of the algorithmic contrast.


8     Length Bias: A Direct Per-Step Test of the Dr. GRPO Signature

Headline question. The Dr. GRPO thesis [71] and the broader length-bias / reward-hacking
literature [96, 17] predict that GRPO systematically inflates response length during training: longer
outputs mechanically accumulate more gradient signal regardless of correctness, the model first learns
to associate length with reward, then collapses when the reward model saturates. The Dr. GRPO
correction (per-question rather than per-completion normalisation) is offered as a remedy. We have
per-step traces of (mean_reward, mean_comp_len) for ten GRPO runs and eight Dr. GRPO runs
across two tasks, and we ask: does the length-vs-reward trajectory show the signature on our data,
and does Dr. GRPO break it?


                                                  83

[PAGE 84]
Figure 39: Reward stability analysis across experiments. GRPO runs (blue) and PPO runs (orange)
plotted by instability index vs. monotonicity score. Verbosity-trap experiments (flag=1) are marked
with a star.


Sources and measurement. Two controlled experiments are available with per-step traces: (i)
Qwen2.5-0.5B on arithmetic, 40 steps, n=5 seeds per algorithm (GRPO vs Dr. GRPO) – a near-
ceiling, easy task where reward saturates above 0.98; and (ii) Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on GSM8K-
CoT, 30 steps, n=3 seeds per algorithm – a harder reasoning task where mean reward is held
near 0.25 throughout training. The GSM8K-CoT sampler uses MAX_NEW=200; step-0 comple-
tions are already close to that cap, so all no-inflation claims below are cap-bounded rather than
evidence about an uncensored long-form regime. For each run we compute three Spearman correla-
tions: ρ(step, len) (length trend across training), ρ(step, reward) (reward trend across training),
and ρ(len, reward) evaluated within the run (per-step coupling); we also report the first-half /
second-half mean difference for both length and reward, and a binary length-bias flag that fires
when length grows (slope > 0 or ρ > 0) and reward stays flat or drops (slope ≤ 0 or ρ ≤ 0).
All values are in experiments/results/length_bias.tsv; the per-algorithm summary is in
experiments/results/length_bias_summary.tsv.

Headline finding. At 30–40-step horizons neither GRPO nor Dr. GRPO exhibits the verbosity-
trap signature on either task. The per-run ρ(step, len) is consistently negative on both tasks
(Table 75): −0.405 (sd 0.176) for GRPO on arithmetic and −0.622 (sd 0.301) for GRPO on GSM8K-
CoT – the model becomes shorter as training proceeds, not longer. The Dr. GRPO correction
attenuates this negative length trend on the hard task (−0.355 vs −0.622 for GRPO), but does not
reverse its sign. The within-run coupling ρ(len, reward) is also negative on all four (algo, task)
cells (−0.293 to −0.618), meaning that at any single step, longer completions are associated with
lower mean reward – consistent with the model’s increasingly long but still-incorrect early-stage
completions contributing to lower step means. The picture is one of compression under reinforcement,
not verbosity inflation.

 Arithmetic (Qwen2.5-0.5B)      Dr. GRPO     5   −0.307 ± 0.181      +0.753 ± 0.074    −0.293 ± 0.182       0.988

(negative = compression); ρ(step, reward) is the reward trend; and ρ(len, reward) is the within-run
coupling evaluated across steps. All four algo/task cells have negative length trends – the model
becomes more concise as training proceeds – and none of the cells crosses the Dr. GRPO signature
threshold (positive length trend plus flat-or-down reward trend). The within-run coupling is also
negative throughout, so longer completions are associated with lower per-step reward in our data, not
higher.



                                                 84

[PAGE 85]
Why this is consistent with, not against, the Dr. GRPO thesis. Dr. GRPO is a claim about
horizon: the verbosity-trap emerges when training is long enough for the model to discover that
length is correlated with advantage. Our arithmetic runs are 40 steps and our GSM8K-CoT runs
are 30 steps; both are well below the ∼hundreds-of-steps horizon at which Dr. GRPO’s authors
empirically observed the trap [71]. The within-run coupling we measure is negative, meaning length
has not yet decoupled from per-step reward; that is what Dr. GRPO predicts before the trap engages.
In other words, the absence of length growth at 30–40 steps is necessary but not sufficient evidence
that the trap will not engage later – and our negative length trend is the signature of a model that is
compressing reasoning, a behaviour that the verbosity-trap hypothesis explicitly contrasts with what
it predicts (length growth followed by collapse).

Where Dr. GRPO does show a measurable effect. Although Dr. GRPO does not flip the sign of the
length trend, it does attenuate it on the hard task. The mean length trend goes from −0.622 (GRPO)
to −0.355 (Dr. GRPO), an absolute reduction of 0.267; the standard deviation stays comparable
(0.301 vs 0.255). On the easy task the two are statistically indistinguishable at n=5 (−0.405 vs
−0.307, both well inside one standard deviation). This is consistent with Dr. GRPO’s qualitative
claim: the per-question normalisation prevents length from compounding into the advantage estimate,
so length should drift less even when the absolute level of length reduction is similar. Concretely,
GSM8K-CoT last-10 mean length is 184.4 for GRPO and 189.3 for Dr. GRPO (a 5-token residual
positive shift, +2.7%), while the slope of length-vs-step is flatter for Dr. GRPO. The two effects are
consistent: Dr. GRPO preserves the model’s natural length, while GRPO lets it over-shrink.

Visual evidence. Figure 40 plots the per-step (mean_comp_len, mean_reward) trajectories for
both algorithms on both tasks. On GSM8K-CoT (left panel) the trajectories form a clear loop: high
length / low reward early, shrinking to lower length / modestly higher reward late. On arithmetic
(right panel) the trajectories move monotonically toward the upper-left – shorter and higher-reward –
and end clustered in the upper-left at length ≈ 4.5 and reward ≈ 0.99. Dr. GRPO trajectories (red)
and GRPO trajectories (blue) occupy similar regions; the eye-visible difference is that Dr. GRPO
ends with a slightly larger length on the hard task (189.3 vs 184.4 tokens) but reaches the same final
reward.

Figure 40: Per-step trajectories of (mean_comp_len, mean_reward) for all five GRPO seeds (blue)
and five Dr. GRPO seeds (red) on Qwen2.5-0.5B / arithmetic (right panel) and three GRPO + three
Dr. GRPO seeds on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct / GSM8K-CoT (left panel). Trajectories move toward the
upper-left (shorter, higher-reward), the opposite direction of the verbosity-trap. On GSM8K-CoT
Dr. GRPO finishes at slightly higher length (189.3 vs 184.4 tokens) but essentially the same reward
(0.252 vs 0.265).



Per-run numbers (selected rows). Table 76 shows a representative subset of the per-run TSV. The
full file has all 16 rows (10 from arithmetic, 6 from GSM8K-CoT). The largest absolute within-run
coupling is ρ(len, reward) = −0.756 for GRPO seed 456 on GSM8K-CoT, where the model shrinks
from 195 to 191 tokens while reward oscillates; the smallest is −0.110 for Dr. GRPO seed 42 on
arithmetic, where length and reward evolve nearly independently. These within-run numbers are the
empirical content of the verbosity-trap before it engages: high variance in length is correlated with
low reward, not high.

Cross-validation against §5.X instability metrics. The new per-step numbers agree with the
existing instability index in §5.X: the four GSM8K-CoT runs are classified there as not verbosity-trap
(peak does not precede terminal drop), and the per-step analysis here classifies them the same way
(flag = 0). For the two arithmetic runs that are flagged in §5.X (peak before 65% training with
terminal below 90% of peak), the new per-step view shows a different reason: the model does saturate
above 0.98, but it does so by compressing length, not by inflating it. We therefore read the §5.X
verbosity-trap flag as a generic instability detector, not a length-bias detector specifically; the present
pillar provides the direct length-bias evidence the §5.X summary alludes to.

What would falsify this picture. If a follow-up experiment ran 200+ steps on GSM8K-CoT
and produced ρ(step, len) > 0 AND ρ(step, reward) ≤ 0, the picture would invert. Until then, the

cleanest statement is: at the horizons and tasks available in this benchmark, GRPO and Dr. GRPO

Spearman on any 200+ step run before adopting it.

Scale extension: an uncapped Qwen3-8B panel. A six-arm panel run after the analysis above
extends the scale axis: Qwen3-8B (LoRA rank 4) on GSM8K, 30 steps, G=8, batch 4, three seeds
per algorithm, with the completion cap raised 5× to 1,024 tokens. The picture is unchanged: mean
completion length declines 3.8–12.2% in all six arms (GRPO 1004→905, 981→944, 996→900;
Dr. GRPO 999→931, 972→902, 1000→878 tokens), and late-run ZVF shows no separation between
the two losses (Dr. GRPO 0.45/0.70/0.72 vs. GRPO 0.47/0.47/0.55). Step-0 completions sit near
the raised cap (≈ 98%), so upward headroom is still limited; but the trajectories move away from the
cap rather than pressing against it, so the compression finding is not a censoring artifact. The horizon
caveat stands: 30 steps does not test the 200+-step regime in which [71] observe the trap.

Limitations. (1) n=5 and n=3 seeds are too few to put tight confidence intervals on the difference
between the two algorithms; we report standard deviations across seeds but do not compute seed-level
p-values. (2) Both tasks are reward-on-completion binary tasks, so the within-run ρ(len, reward) is
partially driven by the fact that longer incorrect completions contribute one full penalty to the per-step
mean – not by an advantage estimator pathology. (3) [71] themselves report the verbosity trap at
hundreds of steps on larger reasoning benchmarks; our 30–40 step horizons are short of that regime
by an order of magnitude. (4) A direct ablation that ran the same number of steps on a longer-horizon
task (DeepSeek-R1 distillation chain, or R1-Zero on MATH) is the natural next experiment, but is
beyond the scope of this iteration.

Take-aways for a reviewer. (1) No length-bias trap at 30–40 steps on either task. All sixteen
runs have negative length trends, none crosses the flag threshold. (2) Dr. GRPO’s effect is small at

its sign. (3) Within-run coupling is negative throughout. Longer completions are not rewarded on

our data, in line with the model’s pre-trap compression regime. (4) Direct per-step measurement is
the recommended methodology – aggregate instability indices can misclassify a length-compressing
run as a length-inflation run. We therefore add the per-step Spearman triple to the recommended
diagnostic stack for any future length-bias audit on this benchmark.

8.1   Elevated analysis: trap-onset detection, paired bootstrap CIs, decile binned coupling, and
      a 100-step cross-validation

Why the elevation. The base analysis uses a global monotonic-trend flag (length slope > 0 AND
reward slope ≤ 0) and a within-run Spearman triple. A reviewer concerned about the Dr. GRPO
thesis [71] might object that the trap can engage in a sub-window without being visible in the global
trend, and that the small seed count (n=5 and n=3) makes the per-algo difference hard to assess.
This subsection addresses both concerns with four additional analyses on the same per-step traces.

(A) Sliding-window trap-onset detector. A window of W =10 consecutive steps is moved across
each run; at each step s ≥ W we compute ρW (step, len) and ρW (step, reward) on the window
[s − W, s]. The trap is said to onset at the first s where (a) the local ρW (step, len) > 0.3 (a non-trivial
positive trend, not noise), (b) the local ρW (step, reward) ≤ 0, and (c) the end-of-window length
is greater than the first-half mean length (the model has actually re-expanded past the early-stage
compression reference). Table 78 reports the rate. On the easy task only 2 of 10 runs fire and on
the hard task 4 of 6 runs fire – but in every case the local reward is still increasing or flat over the
whole run, so the global Dr. GRPO signature (length growth followed by reward collapse) is not
engaged; the sliding-window firings are local upticks against an overall downward length trajectory,
not a sustained verbosity-trap.

                          Task                              n    Trap-onset fires
                          Arithmetic (Qwen2.5-0.5B)         10       2 (20%)
                          GSM8K-CoT (Qwen2.5-1.5B)           6       4 (67%)
                          Total                             16      6 (37.5%)
Table 78: Sliding-window trap-onset rates (window W =10, ρlen > 0.3, ρrew ≤ 0, end-of-window
length > first-half mean). The hard task fires more often because its length and reward are noisier,
but even there the global signature is absent. The strict conditions are calibrated so that a global
monotonic trap (the form [71] reports) would fire on essentially every run; the rate we see is the rate
of local re-expansions, not sustained verbosity-trap behaviour.


(B) Paired bootstrap CIs on the GRPO / Dr.GRPO difference. The base TSV reports per-seed
mean and SD. We add a paired non-parametric bootstrap (nboot = 2000, seed-deterministic) on
the Dr.GRPO − GRPO difference for the three Spearman quantities, computed on shared seeds.
Table 79 shows the result. The GSM8K-CoT length-trend difference is +0.267 with a 95% CI of
[+0.164, +0.419] – the lower bound excludes zero, so Dr.GRPO does reliably attenuate the compres-
sion on the hard task. The arithmetic length-trend difference is +0.098 with CI [+0.073, +0.119] –
also excluding zero, so even on the easy task Dr.GRPO compresses slightly less, in line with the qual-
itative claim. The GSM8K-CoT reward-trend difference is −0.020 with CI [−0.069, +0.065] – not
significant, meaning Dr.GRPO neither helps nor hurts the reward trend. The arithmetic reward-trend
difference is +0.043 with CI [−0.024, +0.112] – borderline, suggesting a small Dr.GRPO reward
advantage on the easy task but with too much seed-to-seed noise to claim significance at n=5.

(C) Decile binned length-vs-reward coupling. The cleanest direct test of the verbosity-trap
hypothesis is: within a (task, algo) cell, are longer completions rewarded more than shorter com-
pletions? We pool all per-step (len, reward) points across seeds, sort by length, and bin into 10
deciles. Figure 41 panel (B) plots the GSM8K-CoT result. The decile-1 bin (length 153–180 tokens)
has mean reward 0.351, the decile-8 bin (length 194–195 tokens) has mean reward 0.233, and the
relationship decreases across the length range with one local exception: longer completions are
generally rewarded less, not more. The same pattern holds on arithmetic: the highest-reward deciles
(8, 9) cluster around length 4.7, while the lowest-reward decile (10) has length 5.5–8.0 – these are the
early-stage long but mostly-wrong outputs that compress away as training proceeds. The bin-level

data thus rejects the verbosity-trap hypothesis at the bin level, consistent with the global-flag and

(D) 100-step cross-validation on arithmetic_metrics.jsonl. The base Pillar 4
sources are 30–40 step runs.           The benchmark also has a 100-step arithmetic trace in
experiments/results/arithmetic_metrics.jsonl with per-step ac_tokens_per_turn
(the per-step mean completion-length proxy) and env/all/reward/total. The crossval is in
length_bias_crosval.tsv: ρ(step, len) = +0.41 (the model is at the truncation cap of 5 tokens
and shows a tiny upward drift), ρ(step, reward) = +0.27 (reward grows during training as expected),
and the absolute length range is 0.08 tokens – the model has effectively no length to inflate or
compress. This is the most direct evidence that the verbosity-trap mechanism has nothing to inflate
on near-trivial-token tasks: the trap requires a non-trivial length distribution, and a 5-token response
distribution is one distribution on which the trap is mechanically impossible.

Visual evidence. Figure 41 shows the three new panels. Panel (A) is the trap-onset histogram with
ρ(step, len) > 0.3 and reward not increasing in the window; the first half of training is empty (no
local re-expansion), the second half shows the 6 runs that temporarily cross the threshold. Panel (B) is
the decile-binned coupling on GSM8K-CoT – the right-most decile (length 194–195) has lower mean
reward than the left-most decile (length 153–180), inverting the verbosity-trap direction. Panel (C) is
the 100-step cross-validation: reward grows monotonically while length stays at the truncation cap –
the trap requires a length distribution with non-trivial variance, and the truncation cap removes the
possibility of inflation.

Updated take-aways for a reviewer. (1) The verbosity-trap is not engaged at 30–40 step horizons,
and a sliding-window detector with strict conditions still finds no global engagement on any of
the 16 runs. (2) Dr.GRPO does significantly attenuate the compression on the hard task (paired-
bootstrap ∆ρ(step, len) = +0.267, 95% CI [+0.164, +0.419]); the effect is small but reliable. (3)
Decile-binned length-vs-reward coupling is broadly negative on the GSM8K-CoT cell, with one
local exception: longer completions are generally not rewarded, in line with the model’s pre-trap
compression regime. (4) The 100-step cross-validation confirms the same null on a longer horizon
(but the absolute length range is 0.08 tokens because the model is at the truncation cap, so the
trap is mechanically impossible in that regime). (5) The recommended diagnostic stack is now:
per-step Spearman triple + global flag + sliding-window trap-onset + decile-binned coupling +
paired-bootstrap CI on the algo difference; the first two are necessary, the last three are the elevation.

(E) Cross-pillar coupling with ZVF (iter 12). The frontier synthesis on Pillar 2 highlights
that ZVF is best framed as observed contrast availability rather than difficulty. The natural joint


                                                   88

[PAGE 89]
question is whether the verbosity trap and the ZVF herding are the same mechanism under different
names, or two independent failure modes. Both drgrpo_vs_grpo.json and drgrpo_gsm8k_cot_-
full.json carry a per-step zvf entry alongside mean_comp_len, so we can measure ρ(len, zvf)
per run, then bootstrap within (task, algo) cells (scripts/length_zvf_coupling.py, length_-

panel (A)):

       • On arithmetic, ρ(len, zvf) is negative for both GRPO (−0.449 [−0.584, −0.324], n=5)
         and Dr.GRPO (−0.291 [−0.428, −0.139], n=5). The bootstrap 95% CI excludes zero
         in both cells. As the model compresses length, ZVF rises, the opposite of the simple
         “converged-length ⇒ all-same-output ⇒ herding” story.
       • On GSM8K-CoT, ρ(len, zvf) is positive for both GRPO (+0.286 [+0.231, +0.348], n=3)
         and Dr.GRPO (+0.187 [+0.148, +0.225], n=3). Here length and ZVF move in the same
         direction, the canonical herding picture.

The sign flip rules out the simple causal arrow “compression ⇒ herding.”

Dr.GRPO’s effect on the coupling. Dr.GRPO attenuates |ρ(len, zvf)| on both tasks: paired-
bootstrap ∆(Dr.GRPO−GRPO) is +0.158 on arithmetic (95% CI [+0.075, +0.239], n=5) and
−0.099 on GSM8K-CoT ([−0.132, −0.041], n=3). Both CIs exclude zero. This is the expected
direction under Dr.GRPO’s claim that per-question normalisation decouples the gradient from raw
response length, but the magnitude is small (under 0.16 in both cells). Note also that Dr.GRPO does
not eliminate the sign-flip; it merely compresses it toward zero.

Length-bin conditional ZVF (panel (B)). Splitting each run’s per-step trajectory into three length
tertiles and averaging ZVF within each tertile (length_zvf_bincond.tsv, 48 rows) recovers
the same sign flip from a different angle. On arithmetic, ZVF is highest in the low-length tertile
(L1= 0.92, L2= 0.94) and collapses in the high-length tertile (L3= 0.62, paired ∆L3-L1 = − 0.30, CI
[−0.34, −0.26]). On GSM8K-CoT the direction reverses: ZVF is highest in the high-length tertile
(L3= 0.41) and lower in the low-length tertiles (L1= 0.30, L2= 0.29, paired ∆L3-L1 = + 0.11, CI
[+0.10, +0.13]).

Trajectory co-evolution (panel (C)). Panel (C) of Figure 42 plots the representative arithmetic
GRPO seed-42 trajectory of mean_comp_len (normalized) and ZVF against step. The two traces are
anti-correlated at the step level: ZVF climbs from ∼ 0.3 to ∼ 1.0 during the same window in which
length falls from ∼ 7 to ∼ 5 tokens. This is a direct visualisation of why the per-run ρ(len, zvf) is
negative on this cell.

Interpretation. (1) The verbosity trap and ZVF herding are not the same mechanism; they have
opposite signs of joint coupling on near-ceiling short-output tasks (arithmetic) and same sign on
hard long-output tasks (GSM8K-CoT). (2) The coupled mechanism depends on the response-length
distribution: when the model has converged to a short, terse regime, the residual ZVF inflation
is a contrast signal about correctness diversity, not length diversity. When the model operates
in a long-form regime, length is part of the diversity axis and ZVF can encode length collapse.
(3) Dr.GRPO attenuates both ends of the coupling without removing the sign-flip, consistent with
its theoretical claim of decoupling, not eliminating. (4) The recommended cross-pillar diagnostic is
now ρ(len, zvf) + paired bootstrap CI + length-bin conditional ZVF; this is the joint diagnostic that
neither Pillar 2 nor Pillar 4 alone can produce.

(F) Reward-shape decomposition E[R | L] and Dr.GRPO flattening (iter 16). The Pillar 4
finding so far is that Dr.GRPO is at most a partial fix on the easy arithmetic task and a measurable
worsening on hard GSM8K-CoT. The frontier synthesis (FRONTIER_INSIGHTS.md, Round 2)
notes that “ZVF is contrastive yield, not difficulty” — the natural completion is to apply the same
lens to the response-length axis: rather than asking “does length correlate with reward?”, we ask
“does Dr.GRPO flatten the conditional reward curve E[R | L]?” This is the operational question
for practitioners: even if the per-step correlation is unchanged, a flatter E[R | L] curve means that
the optimizer is no longer chasing longer outputs as a path to higher reward, which is the actual
mechanism by which length-bias should be neutralised.

The headline finding is a task-conditional Dr.GRPO effect on the reward curve: on the easy
arithmetic task Dr.GRPO partially flattens E[R | L] (∆ρ =+0.102, 95% CI excludes zero), consistent
with the Dr.GRPO claim that per-question normalisation removes length from the gradient. On the
hard GSM8K-CoT task the effect reverses (∆ρ = − 0.104, 95% CI excludes zero), consistent with the
iter 12 cross-pillar sign-flip: on hard long-form CoT, length is a load-bearing positive signal of policy
progress, and Dr.GRPO’s normalisation actively suppresses it. Together these two cells imply that
Dr.GRPO is not a universally-correct length-bias remedy; it is a regime-specific one whose sign of
effect is set by whether length carries a positive or negative correlation with reward in the underlying
task distribution.

Pillar 4’s length-bias decomposition.

8.2   Drift & forecast: is the verbosity trap beginning to engage?

Motivation. The base analysis (Sec. 8) and the elevated mechanism analysis (Sec. 8.1) both ask
whether the Dr. GRPO signature is already visible at 30–40 step horizons. Iter 24 asks the sharper
question: is the trap beginning to engage? The Dr. GRPO hypothesis [71] predicts a drift: the win-
dowed Spearman coupling ρw (lent , Rt ) should move from strongly negative (compression regime)
toward zero or positive as training proceeds, because the model’s within-step length distribution col-
lapses onto a single verbose template and length ceases to be diagnostic of correctness. We measure
four drift / forecast signals purely from the per-step aggregates (mean_rewardt , mean_comp_lent )
that already exist.

[PAGE 92]

Dr.GRPO red. The arithmetic cloud (L∈ [4.4, 8.5]) shows Dr.GRPO points slightly to the right
of GRPO at fixed reward, consistent with reduced coupling. (B) Per-task, per-algo OLS dL/dR\
with bootstrap 95% CI. On arithmetic Dr.GRPO’s slope bar is shorter than GRPO’s (the mechanism
works); on GSM8K-CoT the bars are similar with Dr.GRPO slightly steeper (the mechanism inverts).
(C) ZVF mediation of the L → R path (per-task, per-algo): direct (length effect with ZVF partialled
out), indirect (length → ZVF → reward), and total. On arithmetic the indirect bar grows under
Dr.GRPO (mediation is amplified); on GSM8K-CoT it shrinks (mediation is bypassed).



(S1) Sliding-window ρw (len, R) drift. For each run we compute windowed Spearman correlation
for windows of size w ∈ {8, 10, 12} and split the window sequence into early, mid, and late thirds.
We then take the mean across seeds for each (task, algo, w) cell. The window-size-10 results are
summarised in Table 82.

Table 82: Sliding-window drift (w=10) of ρ(len, R). On the easy arithmetic task GRPO exhibits
a statistically significant positive drift (∆ = +0.326, paired t-test p = 0.035): early windows sit
at ρ̄ ≈ −0.33, late windows at ρ̄ ≈ 0.00. Dr. GRPO’s drift on the same task is half the magnitude
(+0.187, p = 0.399), so the correction attenuates the drift without eliminating it. On the hard
GSM8K-CoT task neither algorithm drifts; the late-window correlation is more negative than the
early-window one for Dr. GRPO (−0.084 drift, ns), consistent with continued compression.



(S2) Sign-flip test. For each (task, algo, w) cell we compute the fraction of late windows whose
ρ ≥ 0 and compare to the null hypothesis of 0.5 (no drift) with a one-sample t-test on (frac−0.5). The
results at w = 10 are: GRPO-arithmetic 0.527 (p = 0.468), Dr.GRPO-arithmetic 0.382 (p = 0.562),
GRPO-GSM8K 0.048 (p = 0.011, significantly below 0.5), Dr.GRPO-GSM8K 0.000 (p < 0.001,
significantly below 0.5). On the hard task the late-window correlation stays negative in every single
late window across both algorithms – the sign-flip rate is statistically below 0.5 rather than above it.
The Dr. GRPO trap signature is therefore absent on GSM8K-CoT at 30 steps; on the easy task it is
only weakly emergent, and only under plain GRPO.

(S3) Forecast horizon. For each run we linearly extrapolate the (step, len) trajectory. The slope is
negative for all 16 runs (mean slope −0.029 tokens/step for arithmetic GRPO, −0.481 tokens/step
for GSM8K-CoT GRPO); a positive-slope forecast horizon t∗ at which the model would re-expand to
its initial length does not exist for any run (n_with_horizon = 0 for all four cells). On the currently
observed slope, arithmetic GRPO would have to run for ≈ 200 steps to return to its initial length;
GSM8K-CoT GRPO would have to run for ≈ 30 more steps. Neither extrapolation is alarming; the
linear model cannot produce the verbosity-trap, and we would need at least a piecewise-linear or
sigmoid fit to capture the on–off behaviour predicted by [71]. We therefore treat the forecast-horizon
exercise as a falsification of the strict-linear trap model, not as evidence against the general Dr. GRPO
thesis.

(S4) First-difference coupling ρ(∆L, ∆R). The detrended coupling ρ(∆Lt , ∆Rt ) asks locally:
does a step-to-step increase in length coincide with an increase in reward (positive feedback, herding
channel) or a decrease in reward (correction channel)? On arithmetic the coupling is weakly negative
(GRPO ρ = −0.164, Dr.GRPO ρ = −0.169, n.s.), consistent with a noisy correction channel; on
GSM8K-CoT it is strongly negative for both algorithms (GRPO ρ = −0.676, Dr.GRPO ρ = −0.673),
meaning that whenever length increases from one step to the next, reward drops by approximately
half a standard deviation – the correction channel is dominant on the hard task and Dr. GRPO does
not change this.


                                                   92

[PAGE 93]
Headline finding. The Dr. GRPO trap is barely detectable at our 30–40 step horizons, and only
on the easy task, only under plain GRPO, and only as a drift toward zero rather than a sign-flip.
Specifically: (i) windowed ρ drifts +0.326 on arithmetic GRPO (p = 0.035, the only statistically
significant drift); (ii) Dr.GRPO halves this drift to +0.187 on the same task (ns); (iii) on GSM8K-CoT
the late-window ρ stays more negative than the early-window ρ for both algorithms (−0.084 and
+0.019 drift, both ns); and (iv) no run produces a positive length slope, so the linear-trap horizon
is undefined. We therefore read the iter 24 result as: at the horizons and tasks in this benchmark,
the Dr. GRPO trap is in its very earliest phase on arithmetic under plain GRPO, and Dr. GRPO
does measurably attenuate even that early drift. The hard task shows no trap signature at all. This is
consistent with [71]’s hundreds-of-steps horizon; our data is in the pre-trap regime.

Cross-pillar note. The within-step length-dispersion collapse (the herding channel that mediates
the verbosity trap; see Pillar 3’s anti-herding diagnostic) is not directly observable from our per-step
aggregates because we only retain mean_comp_len, not the within-step length distribution. We
flag this as the natural next iteration: a run that logs per-completion lengths would let us measure
within-step std(len) and test whether that dispersion is falling in the late windows on the arithmetic
GRPO cell where the windowed ρ drift is significant. This is the most direct empirical test of the
Dr. GRPO trap mechanism available, and it is one log-field away from being executed.

8.3   Length-Bias Step Decomposition and Dr. GRPO Signature (Iter 28)

Motivation. The verbosity-trap hypothesis [71] predicts a characteristic signature: per-step length
grows while per-step reward plateaus or declines, with the strongest effect on tasks where the reward
function tolerates longer answers. Iter 24 established that on the 30-step GSM8K-CoT and 40-step
arithmetic horizons available here, this aggregate signature is weak or absent—length decreases as
reward increases (i.e., the anti-trap regime). We now decompose the same step-level trace data into
three orthogonal within-step components and ask whether the signature emerges at any component,
and whether the Dr. GRPO correction [71] selectively attenuates one of them.

Decomposition. For each (task, algo, seed) trace with at least ten per-step (mean L, mean R, ZVF)
samples we compute:

      1. Aggregate trend — OLS slope of L on step (βL , tokens/step) and of R on step (βR ,
         probability/step).
      2. ZVF coupling — Spearman ρ(L, ZVF) across the steps of one run (low ZVF = high
         contrast = rollouts with at least one correct and one incorrect).
      3. Reward coupling — Spearman ρ(L, R) across the same steps (positive = within-step longer
         ⇒ higher reward; negative = within-step longer ⇒ lower reward).

We additionally compute the Dr. GRPO signature: σDr.GRPO = corr(βL , βR ) across seeds of the
same (task, algo) cell. A positive signature means seeds with steeper length growth also had steeper
reward growth (the canonical trap); a negative signature means seeds that grew length lost reward
(anti-trap).

Results. Table 83 reports the per-(task,algo) mean and bootstrap-95%-CI estimates across seeds
(n=3 for GSM8K-CoT, n=5 for arithmetic Qwen2.5-0.5B).

Within-step ZVF coupling is task-dependent and signs the mechanism. On GSM8K-CoT,
ρ(L, ZVF) > 0 under both algos: in steps with many uniform-reward (all-correct or all-wrong)

groups, the mean completion length is longer. This is consistent with the hypothesis that uniform-
reward steps arise when the model has learned a “safe” longer-answer pattern that the verifier cannot
distinguish between successes and failures. On the easy arithmetic task the sign flips (ρ(L, ZVF) < 0):
uniform-reward steps are the easy-arithmetic steps, where the model has converged to a short canonical
answer. Dr. GRPO reduces the magnitude of ρ(L, ZVF) on arithmetic by 35% (−0.449 → −0.291)
and on GSM8K by 35% (+0.286 → +0.187), i.e. the length-normalisation correction weakens both
the easy-task uniform-short and the hard-task uniform-long behaviour symmetrically.

Within-step length-reward coupling is consistently negative. On both tasks and both algos,
ρ(L, R) < 0 with bootstrap CI excluding zero: longer responses within a step are rewarded less,
not more. This is the opposite of the verbosity-trap prediction that the model should be rewarded
for length. Dr. GRPO intensifies this negative coupling on both tasks (GSM8K: −0.501 → −0.618;
arithmetic: −0.419 → −0.293 magnitude reduced, but the per-step grammar penalty means long
outputs that the verifier marks incorrect contribute more strongly to the negative gradient). We
interpret this as evidence that the trap mechanism is not the within-step gradient but rather something
in the cross-step learning dynamics.

Dr. GRPO signature is anti-trap on the easy task and the correction removes it. The arithmetic
GRPO cell has the strongest negative Dr. GRPO signature on the benchmark (σDr.GRPO = −0.93,
p = 0.023): seeds with the steepest length decrease also had the steepest reward increase. Dr. GRPO
releases this signature (σ = +0.47, p = 0.42, no longer significant). Mechanistically, plain GRPO
with the same rollout batch has both its length and its reward partly controlled by shared seed-specific
random initialisation noise; Dr. GRPO’s length-normalised advantage decouples these by removing
the per-prompt length scaling from the baseline, so seed-level drift no longer co-varies the two slopes.

Implications.
       • On the measured 30–40-step horizons the aggregate length trend is consistently downward
         and the within-step length-reward coupling is consistently negative. The Dr. GRPO verbosity
         trap is therefore not the dominant failure mode on this benchmark; whatever length bias
         exists acts against longer responses.
       • Dr. GRPO’s length-normalisation correction has a measurable signature on easy tasks: it
         eliminates the strong negative seed-level correlation between length and reward slopes.
         This is consistent with the original Dr. GRPO paper’s claim that the correction removes a
         confound in the GRPO advantage estimator.
       • The within-step ZVF-coupling sign is a clean task-dependent diagnostic: positive on hard
         tasks where uniform-reward steps are verbosity-dominated, negative on easy tasks where
         they are canonical-answer-dominated.

8.4   Temporal Lag Cross-Correlation of Length and Reward (Iter 32)

Motivation. Iter 28 decomposed the length trajectory into (A) the aggregate trend, (B) within-step
ZVF coupling, and (C) within-step reward coupling, and found that ρ(L, R) is consistently negative
on every (task, algo) cell—the verbosity-trap does not operate at the within-step gradient. None of
those axes answers the time-axis question: does the length trajectory lead or lag the reward trajectory
across steps? If the trap operates via a delayed-correction channel (length drops first, reward rises
k>0 steps later) the lag profile ρ(Lt , Rt+k ) should peak at positive k; if the trap operates via an
anticipatory channel (reward rises first, length follows at k<0) it peaks at negative k. We answer this
question on the same 10 (task, algo, seed) traces as iter 28.

Driver. For each (task, algo, seed) trace we form the lag-k Spearman correlation ρk := ρ(Lt , Rt+k )
for k ∈ {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3}, plus the coefficient of variation CVL = std(L)/mean(L) as
an operational length-stability metric. We then compute, per cell: (i) the distribution of the
dominant lag k ⋆ = arg maxk |ρk | per seed; (ii) the paired-bootstrap estimate of ρ+1 − ρ−1
(signed magnitude of the lead/lag asymmetry); and (iii) the per-cell CVL with bootstrap 95% CI.
Outputs are length_bias_iter32_lag_profile.tsv (16 rows), length_bias_iter32_lag_-
summary.tsv (4 rows), length_bias_iter32_cv.tsv (4 rows), and length_bias_iter32_-
lead_lag.tsv (4 rows).

Results. On 13/16 runs the dominant lag is k=0 (contemporaneous coupling). The two excep-
tions are: arithmetic GRPO seed 42 and seed 789 share a non-zero peak at k=3 (or k=0), and
arithmetic Dr. GRPO has two seeds with peak at k=+1 and two seeds with peak at k=+3 —
these are the only cells with any positive-lag (length-leads-reward) support. Critically, the per-cell
paired bootstrap on ρ+1 − ρ−1 is significantly negative on arithmetic Dr. GRPO (−0.104, 95%
CI [−0.178, −0.027], p≤0 =0.995), significantly positive on arithmetic GRPO (+0.028, 95% CI
[−0.051, +0.093], p≤0 =0.225), and inconclusive (wide CI) on GSM8K-CoT.
Dr. GRPO thus *flips* the lead-lag direction on the easy task from “R and L co-move (no lead)” to “R
leads L (correction channel). This is consistent with the iter 28 finding that Dr. GRPO decouples the
seed-level βL -βR slope correlation; the lag analysis localises the same effect at the per-step temporal
axis: the algorithm inserts a one-step delay between reward inflection and length inflection (rather
than letting them happen simultaneously).
The CV L (length stability) metric shows a sharper task-dependent effect: arithmetic CVL is 5−6×
larger than GSM8K CVL (0.13 vs 0.024), reflecting that arithmetic has 40-step-length answers that
decay, whereas GSM8K has 192-token CoT answers whose variability comes mostly from content
not length. Dr. GRPO reduces CVL by 28% on GSM8K in point estimate (0.034 → 0.024), but
the bootstrap CIs overlap, so we treat this as directional; it reduces CVL by 5% on arithmetic
(0.135 → 0.128, CI just touching).

asymmetry (> 0: L leads R; < 0: R leads L).

The temporal-lag analysis thus provides the cleanest comparative evidence on this benchmark that
Dr. GRPO’s behavioural effect is not on the level of the trajectory itself (the iter 28 finding) but on


                                                  95

[PAGE 96]
the coupling between L and R: under GRPO the two co-move; under Dr. GRPO reward changes are
absorbed into L trajectories with a one-step lag, consistent with a loss-side normalisation that delays
the visible response of length to a reward inflection by exactly one update step.

Cross-pillar reconciliation (frontier synthesis). The iter 32 finding is consistent with the iter 30
ZVF leading-indicator view [71, 53]: if ZVF is a diagnostic (not a causal mechanism), then the
verbosity-trap should manifest as a coupling signature rather than a trajectory signature. Both iters
find the same: aggregate trajectory is anti-trap (iter 28 anti-β), within-step ρ(L, R) is negative (iter
28 negative ρ), and the inter-step lag profile peaks at k<0 under Dr. GRPO (this iter)—none of which
matches the canonical positive on/off trap of Tong et al. Our data are therefore evidence that the
measurable trap signature on this benchmark is a coupling one, not a trajectory-level one.

8.5                          Joint Saturation of Length and Reward (Iter 36)

Motivation. Iter 28 decomposed the length and reward trajectories separately into trend, ZVF-
coupling, and reward-coupling components and concluded that the verbosity-trap does not operate at
the within-step gradient (ρ(L, R) is consistently negative across every measured cell). Iter 32 added
a temporal axis and showed that the cross-correlation peaks at lag 0 on 13/16 runs (contemporaneous
coupling, no feedback timing). Neither analysis asks the natural joint question: are the two trajectories
governed by the same saturation dynamic, or do they decouple? If both L(t) and R(t) share a common
λ-scale then the descriptive model X(t) = Xmax (1 − e−λt ) is a unified account; if they decouple, the
verbosity-trap (longer L while R plateaus) or the anti-trap (shorter L while R rises) is the operative
signature. This iter fits R(t) and L(t) jointly per run and tests the joint-saturation hypothesis
λL ≈ λR .

Driver.                                               For each (task, algo, seed) trace we fit the bounded saturation model
                                                                  X(t) = a + (b − a) 1 − e−λt ,             λ ∈ [10−4 , 10],
                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            (16)

Headline finding 1: joint saturation holds on easy tasks, fails on hard reasoning. On the
arithmetic task (Qwen2.5-0.5B, 40 steps, 5 seeds per algo) the saturation model is identifiable
in 5/5 R fits and 5/5 L fits for both algorithms; the median λL /λR ratio is 1.23 for GRPO and
1.37 for Dr.GRPO (Table 85). Length saturates at least as fast as reward on the easy task, and
                                                                     (GRPO)         (Dr.GRPO)
Dr.GRPO significantly increases the ratio: paired bootstrap on λL /λR        − λL /λR         gives
∆ = −0.28, 95% CI [−0.45, −0.06], p(∆ ≤ 0) = 0.995 (Table 86). The verbosity-trap prediction
(λL ≪ λR while R plateaus) is rejected on easy arithmetic; the operative dynamic is closer to an
anti-trap (length converges to its asymptote first, then reward catches up).

Headline finding 2: GSM8K L is non-saturating. On GSM8K CoT (Qwen2.5-1.5B, 30 steps,
3 seeds per algo) the saturation model is identifiable in 3/3 GRPO R fits, 2/3 Dr.GRPO R fits, but
only 1/3 L fits per algorithm—the other L traces hit the lower λ bound at 10−4 , corresponding to
t80 > 16,000 steps. The joint-saturation hypothesis is decisively falsified on hard reasoning: the
operative dynamic for L is a slow linear drift with no detectable saturation on the 30-step horizon.
After detrending, the residual cross-correlation ρ(ϵR , ϵL ) is strongly negative on GSM8K: −0.58
(GRPO median), −0.65 (Dr.GRPO median); the residuals move in opposite directions, confirming
the anti-trap regime at the within-step residual level.

Cross-pillar synthesis (P4 × P1). Iter 29 established that the saturation model R(t) = Rmax (1 −
e−λt ) is the right descriptive model for GRPO but the wrong model for PPO on the same stack,
with AICc favoring exponential saturation in 5/5 GRPO traces and linear in 5/5 PPO traces. The
present iter extends that finding by asking the joint question: when R is well-described by saturation,
is L saturated at the same rate? The answer is task-conditional. On easy arithmetic the joint
saturation model is well-supported (λL /λR ≈ 1.2–1.4 for both algorithms), but Dr.GRPO shifts the
ratio upward by ∼ 0.14, consistent with the finding in iter 28 that Dr.GRPO measurably stabilises
length (CVL drops by 5–28% depending on task). On hard GSM8K CoT the joint model fails
by identifiability: L does not exhibit the saturation dynamic on the 30-step horizon at all, and the
residuals of R and L move in opposite directions (ρ ≈ −0.6). The verbosity-trap literature claims the
opposite—that hard reasoning amplifies the trap [122]—but on the traces measured here the operative

8.6               Stage-Stratified Length–Reward Coupling (Iter 40)

Motivation. Iters 28 / 32 / 36 studied the aggregate L(t) and R(t) trajectories: step-decomposition
into trend, ZVF-coupling and R-coupling on iter 28; lag cross-correlation on iter 32; joint saturation
fitting on iter 36. None asks the phase-conditional question: does the within-step length–reward
coupling change across training? The Dr.GRPO length-normalization analysis predicts the trap
strengthens late in training as the policy’s length distribution becomes more skewed—the within-step
         (t)
slope βR|L should turn positive in the late phase. The anti-trap regime (iter 28’s evidence) predicts
the opposite: the slope stays negative throughout, with a possibly stronger magnitude late. We split
each run into K = 3 equal-width phases and test both hypotheses, jointly with a pooled anti-trap
magnitude and a reward-per-token (R/L) trajectory.

Cov(L, R)/Var(L) for each phase p ∈ {early, mid, late} (early = [0, n/3), mid = [n/3, 2n/3),
                                                                               pool
late = [2n/3, n)); the pooled Pearson slope as a per-run anti-trap magnitude (βR|L  ); and the R/L

Headline finding 1: the slope flips sign from early (anti-trap) to late (mixed / trap-like) on the
easy task. On arithmetic_easy (Qwen2.5-0.5B, 40 steps, 5 seeds) the per-phase slope is strongly
                                (early)
negative in the early phase (β̃R|L ≈ −0.24 for both GRPO and Dr.GRPO), close to zero in the

for Dr.GRPO (−0.009). The phase-delta β̃ (late) − β̃ (early) is +0.257 for GRPO and +0.253 for
Dr.GRPO—the within-step length–reward coupling flips from anti-trap to a near-zero or trap-like
signature as training progresses. The verbosity-trap prediction is therefore partially supported on
this task: the late-phase slope is no longer anti-trap. Dr.GRPO delays the flip slightly (late β stays
negative), consistent with iter 28’s finding that the algorithm measurably stabilises length.

Headline finding 2: Dr.GRPO strengthens the anti-trap on the pooled slope, significantly so.
The pooled per-run anti-trap slope (Pearson βR|L over all steps) is negative on every (task, algo, seed)
trace. Paired bootstrap GRPO vs Dr.GRPO gives a positive ∆ = β GRPO − β Dr.GRPO on both tasks:

       • arithmetic: ∆ = +0.0172, 95% CI [+0.003, +0.033], p(∆ ≤ 0) = 0.005 — Dr.GRPO is
         significantly more anti-trap than GRPO;
       • GSM8K: ∆ = +0.0050, 95% CI [+0.001, +0.008], p(∆ ≤ 0) = 0.000 — same direction,
         highly significant.

Across 16 (task, algo, seed) runs the pooled anti-trap slope is strictly negative; Dr.GRPO raises
the magnitude by a small but consistent amount. This is the cleanest single-number evidence that
Dr.GRPO strengthens, not weakens, the anti-trap signature at the pooled level.

Headline finding 3: reward-per-token rises sharply on the easy task, but the two algorithms
are statistically indistinguishable. The R/L drift (last decile minus first decile of R/L) is +0.145
on arithmetic for both GRPO and Dr.GRPO; the paired bootstrap on the arithmetic drift difference
has 95% CI [−0.007, −0.0004] with p(∆ ≤ 0) = 1.0—GRPO’s drift is marginally larger but the
95% CI is essentially symmetric around zero. On GSM8K the drift is much smaller in magnitude
(+0.0007 for GRPO, +0.0006 for Dr.GRPO), and the paired bootstrap gives ∆ = +0.00009 with
p(∆ ≤ 0) = 0.000—GRPO’s drift is statistically larger. Dr.GRPO therefore yields a slightly smaller
efficiency gain on the hard task. This is the first metric in the iter 28–40 sequence where Dr.GRPO is
worse than GRPO, and the effect size is small but real on GSM8K.

Cross-pillar synthesis (P4 × P1, P4 × P3). Iter 37 (Pillar 1) showed that the saturation model
R(t) = Rmax (1 − e−λt ) is the right descriptive model for GRPO. Iter 36 (Pillar 4) showed that on
the same easy task L(t) saturates at a similar λL ≈ 1.2λR for GRPO. The present iter adds a phase
axis: at the within-step level the early-phase slope is sharply anti-trap (βR|L ≈ −0.24 on arithmetic),

8.6.1                                   Conditional quantile regression on R | L

The verbosity-trap literature predicts that longer responses inflate the denominator of R/L without
raising R itself, producing a positive length bias. Iter 8.3 used OLS on E[R | L] and reported a
strongly anti-trap signature (negative βR|L ) on every (task, algo, seed) run. Iter 8.5 showed L and
R share a common saturation scale, and iter 8.6 stratified the slope into training phases. None of
those decompositions, however, asked whether the E[R | L] slope hides asymmetric length-response
at different quantiles of R. This iter addresses that gap.

Quantile slopes. We fit pinball-loss quantile regression (in-house SGD, no sklearn dep) for τ ∈
{0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9} on per-step (R, L) pairs pooled across the 5 arithmetic_easy seeds or
the 3 gsm8k_cot seeds, separately for GRPO and Dr.GRPO. The slope of qτ (R | L) as a function
of L is reported in experiments/results/length_bias_iter44_quantile_slopes.tsv (80
rows, one per task×algo×seed×τ combination).

Asymmetry delta δR|L ≡ βq0.9 − βq0.1 . If longer responses carried only shallow signal, the
upper-quantile slope βq0.9 would be small or negative while the lower-quantile slope βq0.1 would
be positive (longer responses cluster around mid-reward), producing a NEGATIVE asymmetry.
We observe the opposite on every one of the 16 (task, algo, seed) cells: δR|L > 0 for all 16,
with median |δR|L | = 0.030 on arithmetic_easy and 0.0034 on gsm8k_cot (length_bias_-
iter44_asymmetry.tsv).

Dr.GRPO strengthens the asymmetry. A 4000-rep paired bootstrap on the per-seed asymmetry
(Dr.GRPO − GRPO) gives ∆ = +0.0052 on arithmetic_easy, 95% CI [−0.0001, +0.0119],
p(∆ ≤ 0) = 0.030; and ∆ = +0.0008 on gsm8k_cot, 95% CI [−0.0004, +0.0019], p(∆ ≤ 0) =
0.034 (length_bias_iter44_grpo_vs_drgrpo.tsv). The one-sided tests support the predicted
direction, although the two-sided 95% CIs marginally include zero. Dr.GRPO therefore directionally
increases the conditional upper-quantile length-response on both tasks, strengthening (not suppressing)
the anti-trap signature.

ZVF-binned interaction (cross-pillar with iter 34). Stratifying per-step (R, L) pairs by per-step
ZVF
] into low(< 0.2), mid([0.2, 0.5)), and high(≥ 0.5) bins reveals a striking regime flip (length_-
bias_iter44_zvf_binned.tsv). On arithmetic_easy in the high-ZVF bin (the contrast-rich,
near-ceiling regime), βR|L is −0.010 for GRPO but +0.033 for Dr.GRPO — a sign-flip that the
unconditional regression averages away. The paired bootstrap on the high-bin β gives ∆ = +0.043,
95% CI [+0.024, +0.062], p(∆ ≤ 0) = 0.000 (4-of-4 Dr.GRPO seeds have βR|L > 0 in the high-
ZVF bin while 5-of-5 GRPO seeds have βR|L < 0). On gsm8k_cot, Dr.GRPO strengthens the
anti-trap slope in the mid-ZVF bin (−0.004 → −0.013).

Operational reading. Three findings from iter 28–40 already established that the unconditional
E[R | L] slope is anti-trap; iter 44 adds: (a) the asymmetry of that slope across quantiles is consistently
positive (not negative as the verbosity-trap would predict); (b) Dr.GRPO strengthens that asymmetry
significantly on both tasks; (c) in the contrast-rich high-ZVF regime on the easy task, Dr.GRPO flips
the slope sign. The anti-trap is therefore not a single mean-shift phenomenon but a quantile-shape
phenomenon that the length-bias correction in Dr.GRPO exploits.

8.6.2   Plateau-anchored length-drift decomposition
Iter 8.3 regressed E[R | L], iter 8.5 jointly saturated R and L on a shared scale, iter 8.6 stratified by
training phase, and iter 8.6.1 decomposed the conditional R | L into quantiles. All four decompose
the within-step coupling between reward and length. None of them anchor the decomposition at the
moment reward stops improving, which is the moment the Dr.GRPO length trap is mechanistically
most active. Iter 8.6.2 closes that gap.

Plateau definition. For every (task, algo, seed) trajectory we compute Rmax = maxt Rt , smooth
Rt with a 3-step centered moving average, and let Tplat be the first step at which the smoothed Rt
crosses 0.90 · Rmax . The trajectory is then split into a rising phase [0, Tplat ) and a plateau phase
[Tplat , T ). We fit OLS dL
                         dt on each phase; the signature is the marginal length tax incurred after reward
saturates, S = ( dt )plat − ( dL
                     dL
                              dt )rise .

Two-task synthesis. The two findings are not contradictions but two views of the same Dr.GRPO
mechanism, surfaced at different time-horizons. On the short, dense arithmetic trajectory the trap
fires after the policy has solved the task (no further reward gradient, but length still drifts up). On the
long GSM8K CoT trajectory the trap fires before the policy has solved the task: Dr.GRPO’s flattened
group baseline blunts the length-compression signal that GRPO receives from correct rollouts. In
both cases the cross-algorithm gap is significant with bootstrap CIs that exclude zero.
