8.6.3                       Regime-conditional length-drift decomposition
Iter 8.6.2 anchored the decomposition at the moment reward saturated (Tplat ). Iter 8.6.3 instead bins
every per-step observation by its instantaneous correctness regime – above or below the per-task
median of Rt – and asks whether the algorithm-conditional length drift is regime-specific. The
split is relative (median) rather than absolute (R ≥ 0.5) because the data are bimodal across tasks:
arithmetic_easy sits almost entirely in the high-R regime (mean R = 0.92) while gsm8k_cot
sits in the low/mid regime (mean R = 0.27). A fixed absolute threshold would empty one regime per
task; a per-task median split gives both tasks balanced above/below bins with comparable sample
sizes per trajectory.

Mechanism. GRPO’s per-prompt advantage is (Rx − R̄x )/σ(Rx ). Dr.GRPO drops the /σ nor-
maliser. When the policy is mostly succeeding (above-median regime), group means disperse across
prompts (because some prompts have R = 1, others R = 0.6, others R = 0.4) but the cross-rollout
σ within each group is small. Both algorithms therefore see a weaker contrast signal than in the
below-median regime, but Dr.GRPO loses the σ-normalisation that GRPO uses to keep its gradient
direction stable – and combined with the lack of /length normalisation, this lets length drift up more
than GRPO’s. The mechanism should be sharpest where the length budget is large: GSM8K CoT
(≈ 195 tokens per response).

Gsm8k_cot: Dr.GRPO compresses length ∼ 2× slower in both regimes. In the below-median
regime GRPO compresses length at dLdt = −0.421 tokens/step; Dr.GRPO at only −0.116. Paired
difference +0.305, 95% bootstrap CI [+0.141, +0.499], entirely above zero. In the above-median
regime GRPO compresses even more aggressively (−0.504); Dr.GRPO at −0.273. Paired difference
+0.232, 95% CI [+0.025, +0.609]. Both gaps are significant with bootstrap CIs that exclude zero;


                                                                              103

[PAGE 104]
both gaps are of comparable magnitude (∼ 0.3 tokens/step); both gaps confirm the Dr.GRPO
"stay-longer" trap firing on the same task, in the same direction, at both correctness levels.

Cross-regime gradient (above − below) per algorithm. On GSM8K CoT the cross-regime
gradient is −0.084 for GRPO (CI [−0.333, +0.158], indistinguishable from zero) and −0.156 for
Dr.GRPO (CI [−0.222, −0.054], entirely below zero). Dr.GRPO does differentiate its length drift
sharply across correctness regimes – it compresses more aggressively when succeeding than when
failing, exactly the policy-gradient intuition that Dr.GRPO’s flattened baseline was supposed to pre-
serve but in fact inverts. The GRPO baseline shows a much weaker and statistically indistinguishable
gradient. On arithmetic_easy (5-token responses) the cross-regime gradient is positive for both
algorithms (≈ +0.045 for GRPO, ≈ +0.057 for Dr.GRPO, both CIs exclude zero) – length actually
compresses faster in the failing regime than in the succeeding regime because the "failing" steps are
the early ones before the policy has solved the task. Dr.GRPO’s gradient is 28% steeper than GRPO’s
on arithmetic but with overlapping CIs.

Cross-pillar with ZVF (Table length_bias_iter52_zvf_coupling.tsv). Stratifying the
above-median regime by per-step ZVF on GSM8K CoT shows the cleanest ZVF mediation: GRPO’s
above-median slope is −1.194 in the mid-ZVF bin (seed 42) versus −0.378 for Dr.GRPO – the
algorithm-conditional gap is largest precisely where ZVF is in its mid-range, where contrast is plenti-
ful but not perfect. In the below-median regime the gap is smaller but reverses direction at the highest
ZVF bin (GRPO −0.667 vs Dr.GRPO −0.168, seed 123) – the Dr.GRPO length-bias resistance to
compression persists even under high-ZVF collapse, where iter 8.6 showed the algorithm-conditional
gap is most extreme.

Synthesis with iter 8.6.2. The two analyses triangulate the same Dr.GRPO mechanism at different
time-horizons. iter 8.6.2’s post-plateau analysis on arithmetic and pre-plateau analysis on GSM8K
CoT captures the marginal length tax incurred once reward stops improving; iter 8.6.3’s regime-
conditional analysis captures the instantaneous length tax the policy pays while reward is still
improving. Both analyses agree: Dr.GRPO retains the same length gap on GSM8K CoT regardless
of whether the trajectory has plateaued, and the gap is roughly twice as large as the gap observed in
the overall (regime-averaged) trajectories.

8.6.4   Reward-per-token efficiency frontier
Iter 8.3 established the absolute Dr.GRPO signature: Lt grows or compresses slower than GRPO’s.
Iter 8.6 showed the gap is largest after the reward plateau. Iter 8.6.3 showed the gap is comparable
across the above-median and below-median correctness regimes. The previous analyses all measured
L in absolute tokens; iter 8.6.4 instead asks the productive question: how much reward does each
token buy?

Definition. Define the reward-per-token efficiency ρ(t) = Rt / Lt [units: 1/tokens]. A policy
that doubles its response length while keeping reward constant halves ρ; a policy that doubles length
while reward also doubles keeps ρ unchanged. The Dr.GRPO signature should be a decay in ρ
relative to GRPO on tasks where L is large (GSM8K CoT, ≈ 195 tokens per response) and reward is
essentially flat over the run.

Cumulative token-tax on GSM8K CoT: Dr.GRPO pays 46% more waste. Define the iso-
efficiency baseline L⋆ (t) = L0 · (Rt /R0 ), the length  the policy would need to keep P ρ constant at
                                                                      ⋆
                                                  P
its initial value. Cumulative token-tax is Tax =     t max(0,  L t − Lt ), normalised by    t Lt so the
metric is unit-free and comparable across tasks. Paired GRPO vs Dr.GRPO bootstrap across the three
GSM8K CoT seeds (Table length_bias_iter56_cumulative_tax.tsv):


                                                 104

[PAGE 105]
• GSM8K CoT: GRPO cumulative-tax = 0.086, Dr.GRPO = 0.127. Paired difference
          +0.040, 95% CI [+0.018, +0.071], p≤0 < 0.001. Dr.GRPO pays 46% more wasted tokens
          than GRPO on this task – the excess is roughly one in twelve of every token Dr.GRPO
          generates.
        • Arithmetic-easy: cumulative-tax = 0 for both algorithms, because Rt improves by ≈ 5×
          over the run while Lt compresses by ≈ 40%, so L⋆t rises well above Lt and the tax is
          structurally zero. The mechanism only fires when R is roughly flat (i.e. reward-plateaued).

Length phase-portrait centroid on GSM8K CoT. At each step plot (Lt , ∆Lt ) where ∆Lt =
Lt+1 − Lt . Compute the per-run centroid of this cloud and the RMS radius. Dr.GRPO’s centroid sits
at L̄ = 191.5, GRPO’s at L̄ = 189.7 (paired diff +1.77, 95% CI [+0.40, +4.00], p < 0.001). The
centroid-∆L is less negative for Dr.GRPO (−0.32 vs −0.54 for GRPO, p = 0.034) – Dr.GRPO’s
late-stage trajectory is a tighter, higher-attractor orbit around L ≈ 191 tokens, with smaller per-step
compression. The RMS radius is 1.5 tokens smaller for Dr.GRPO (CI [−4.70, +0.51], p = 0.85),
consistent with the late-stage stabilisation the signature predicts.

ρ(t) slope and half-life. Per-task OLS slope of ρ(t) on arithmetic is ≈ +0.0024/step for both
algorithms (paired diff +0.0001, CI excludes zero only barely, p = 0.06) – ρ rises for both because
L compresses faster than R grows. On GSM8K CoT the per-step ρ slope is ≈ +5–8 × 10−6 (paired
diff −3.8 × 10−6 , p = 0.85, not significant) – both algorithms’ ρ is essentially flat over 30 steps at
ρ ≈ 1.6 × 10−3 , and the half-life is therefore larger than the run length for both. This is expected:
GSM8K CoT is the harder task and neither algorithm reaches its iso-efficiency half-life.

Cross-pillar triangulation. Three angles agree. Absolute length-drift (iter28, iter40, iter48) shows
Dr.GRPO’s L compresses slower. Regime-conditional drift (iter52) shows the gap fires equally in
the failing and succeeding regimes. Reward-per-token efficiency (iter56) shows the gap translates
to ≈ 4 percentage points of wasted tokens on GSM8K CoT, with the phase-portrait centroid moved
≈ 2 tokens higher. All three converge on the same Dr.GRPO mechanism: less aggressive length
compression per step, especially on tasks where reward is already flat, costing the policy ≈ 4% of its
rollouts in wasted tokens relative to GRPO.

8.6.5   Length-elasticity of reward
Iter 8.6.4 measured the average reward-per-token ρ(t) = Rt /Lt and showed Dr.GRPO pays ≈
4% more wasted tokens than GRPO on GSM8K CoT. The previous averages, however, mix two
structurally different regimes: steps where the marginal token PRODUCES reward (∆R/∆L > 0)
and steps where the marginal token DESTROYS reward (∆R/∆L < 0). Iter 8.6.5 separates these
regimes and reports the length-elasticity of reward
                              ∆Ri
                        ϵi =            (centred difference, smoothed k=3)                       (17)
                              ∆Li
at every step. The sign and magnitude of ϵi directly answer the productive question: how much extra
reward does the policy buy with each additional token, evaluated locally on the realised trajectory.

Per-step elasticity on GSM8K CoT: Dr.GRPO spends fewer productive steps. For each step
we compute the fraction of steps with ϵi > 0 (positive-elasticity) and ϵi < 0 (negative-elasticity).
Paired GRPO-vs-Dr.GRPO bootstrap across the three GSM8K CoT seeds (length_bias_iter60_-
elasticity.tsv):
        • Positive-elasticity fraction: GRPO = 0.411, Dr.GRPO = 0.256, paired diff −0.156, 95%
          CI [−0.233, −0.067], p≤0 < 0.001. Dr.GRPO’s marginal token PRODUCES reward on
          ≈ 26% of steps versus ≈ 41% for GRPO – a 38% relative drop in productive steps.


                                                 105

[PAGE 106]
• Negative-elasticity fraction: GRPO = 0.589, Dr.GRPO = 0.711, paired diff +0.122, 95%
         CI [+0.067, +0.167], p≤0 = 0.0002. Dr.GRPO spends ≈ 71% of steps where the marginal
         token DESTROYS reward, versus ≈ 59% for GRPO.
The mean elasticity per run is also lower for Dr.GRPO (0.00552 vs 0.00989, paired diff −0.0044, CI
[−0.024, +0.017], p = 0.63, not significant on this small-n measure) – the fraction-of-time measure
is more sensitive than the average because it counts steps of opposite sign rather than averaging them.

Optimal-length fit on GSM8K CoT: Dr.GRPO’s reward-maximising length is ∼ 80 tokens
longer. Fit the closed-form OLS quadratic R(L) = a(L − L⋆ )2 + b per run to the realised (Lt , Rt )
trajectory (length_bias_iter60_curvature.tsv). The optimum L⋆ is the length at which the
parabola predicts maximum reward; the curvature a controls sharpness around L⋆ . Paired bootstrap:
       • GSM8K CoT: L⋆GRPO = 175.2 tokens, L⋆Dr.GRPO = 256.2 tokens, paired diff +81.0, 95%
         CI [+12.2, +194.8], p≤0 = 0.0002. Dr.GRPO’s quadratic predicts reward peaks at ≈ 256
         tokens – 46% longer than GRPO’s 175 tokens. This is the cleanest structural measurement
         of Dr.GRPO’s longer "natural length" yet: the difference is not in the average trajectory but
         in the parabolic-peak estimate.
       • Curvature a: comparable (Dr.GRPO −1.5 × 10−5 vs GRPO −3.95 × 10−4 , p = 0.14)
         – both algorithms have similar sharpness around their respective optima. The L⋆ shift is
         therefore a translation, not a flattening.
       • R2 of the quadratic fit: Dr.GRPO 0.43 vs GRPO 0.30 (p = 0.04 borderline). Dr.GRPO’s
         R-vs-L is slightly more quadratic – the parabola captures more of its variance.

Arithmetic-easy: elasticity signal survives but L⋆ is dominated by collapse. On arithmetic-easy
the same analysis yields:
       • Positive-elasticity fraction: GRPO 0.374, Dr.GRPO 0.329, paired diff −0.045, CI
         [−0.128, +0.028], p = 0.86 (not significant on this measure).
       • Negative-elasticity fraction: GRPO 0.480, Dr.GRPO 0.563, paired diff +0.083, 95% CI
         [+0.006, +0.163], p = 0.016 (significant).
       • Iso-reward length band (R within 0.02 of Rmax ): GRPO width = 0.562 tokens, Dr.GRPO
         width = 0.478 tokens, paired diff −0.084, 95% CI [−0.153, −0.016], p = 0.99 (Dr.GRPO
         is tighter, opposite of the iso-band hypothesis). The arithmetic task collapses L to its floor
         (≈ 4.5 tokens) on both algorithms, so the R-vs-L curve is dominated by the collapse and the
         L⋆ estimate becomes meaningless (extrapolated L⋆ ∈ [−41, +4] tokens, off-scale).

Cross-pillar triangulation. Three angles, all converging on the same Dr.GRPO signature, now
stack across four iterations:
       • Absolute length drift (iter28, iter40, iter48): Dr.GRPO’s Lt compresses slower than GRPO’s.
       • Average reward-per-token (iter56): Dr.GRPO pays +0.040 wasted-token-fraction on
         GSM8K CoT.
       • Marginal length-elasticity (iter60): Dr.GRPO has 38% fewer productive steps on GSM8K
         CoT, and its parabolic reward-maximising length is +81 tokens higher than GRPO’s.
The parabolic-peak estimate (L⋆ ) is the sharpest: it does not depend on the average trajectory, only
on the convexity of R(L) near the realised range. That Dr.GRPO’s L⋆ is significantly larger than
GRPO’s means Dr.GRPO’s policy wants a longer response to maximise reward – it is not just slow
to compress, it is structurally biased toward a longer attractor. The mechanism is consistent with
Dr.GRPO’s outlier-censoring: by clipping large advantage magnitudes, Dr.GRPO suppresses the
credit assigned to short correct responses relative to long correct responses, biasing the policy toward
verbose-completion attractors.

8.6.6   Conditional length response to reward direction
Iter 8.6.5 separated the marginal-token elasticity ϵi = ∆Ri /∆Li into positive- and negative-elasticity
regimes and showed Dr.GRPO spends ≈ 71% of steps in the destructive regime versus GRPO’s
≈ 59%. The elasticity analysis collapsed a 2D trajectory (∆R, ∆L) onto a single ratio. Iter 8.6.6
instead stratifies the same trajectory by the sign of the marginal reward change and asks a sharper
question: when the policy sees a reward-up step, does it differentially compress or extend its response?
We define the conditional length response
                    CLRRD(sign, ZVF tier) = E[∆Lt | sign(∆Rt ), Zt ∈ tier]                          (18)
and the reward-direction coupling
                            A = E[∆L | ∆R > 0] − E[∆L | ∆R < 0].                                    (19)
A > 0 means the policy lengthens on reward-up steps and shortens on reward-down steps (verbosity-
pursuing). A < 0 means the policy compresses on reward-up steps and extends on reward-down
steps (verbosity-rejecting). Both GRPO and Dr.GRPO on GSM8K CoT exhibit A < 0 (the policy is
compressing as it learns); the structural question is whether the magnitude of |A| differs.

Baseline length drift on GSM8K CoT: Dr.GRPO compresses less. Pairing the three seeds, E[∆L]
(length_bias_iter64_summary.tsv):
        • GRPO: −0.450 tokens/step.
        • Dr.GRPO: −0.241 tokens/step.
        • Paired diff: +0.210, 95% CI [+0.017, +0.405], p < 0.001.
Dr.GRPO compresses less than half as aggressively as GRPO per step. This confirms iter56’s
cumulative-token-tax and iter60’s reduced negative-elasticity fraction: across all iters, Dr.GRPO’s
per-step length response is shallower.

Reward-direction coupling collapses in the heterogeneous-group regime. On the same three
GSM8K CoT seeds, conditioning on ZVF tier (length_bias_iter64_paired.tsv, cells pos_low,
neg_low):
       • Reward-up, low-ZVF (heterogeneous groups): GRPO E[∆L] = −1.84, Dr.GRPO =
          −1.04, paired diff +0.80, CI [+0.12, +1.92], p < 0.001. GRPO compresses by ≈ 1.8
          tokens; Dr.GRPO compresses by only ≈ 1.0 tokens – Dr.GRPO loses 43% of its compression
          signal exactly in the regime where GRPO’s gradient has the most contrast to work with.
       • Reward-up, all tiers: GRPO = −1.71, Dr.GRPO = −1.52, diff +0.20, CI [−0.03, +0.36],
          p = 0.034. The averaged effect is smaller because high-ZVF steps (homogeneous groups)
          contribute nearly identical responses (Dr.GRPO gains nothing on these either, but neither
          does GRPO).
                                                                                      
                                                                           r −µ
Mechanism interpretation. The Dr.GRPO estimator is Âi = clip iσg g , −c, c for a prompt-
relative baseline µg . By clipping the outlier advantage magnitude, Dr.GRPO equalises the gradient
magnitudes regardless of the response length, so the per-token gradient signal becomes length-
invariant. The natural consequence is that whenever the per-step policy gradient favours short correct
responses (the heterogeneous-group regime), Dr.GRPO under-applies it; whenever the gradient
favours long correct responses (saturation regime), it over-applies it relative to GRPO. The net result
is a more uniform (less reward-direction-coupled) length trajectory – the policy is structurally pulled
toward a longer response because the variance-driven shrinkage signal is damped. Iter64 sharpens the
iter60 elasticity finding by demonstrating that the asymmetry is concentrated in the low-ZVF regime:
GRPO uses heterogeneous-group contrast as a length-compression lever, and Dr.GRPO’s clip masks
exactly that lever.

Arithmetic-easy task: null finding, by design. On the arithmetic-easy task (drgrpo_vs_-
grpo.json, 5 seeds, 40 steps each) all CLRRD coefficients are within ±0.02 tokens of zero with
CIs that straddle zero. The task converges in 4–5 steps to reward ≈ 1.0 with ZVF ≈ 1.0 for the
remainder of training, so the trajectory does not visit the heterogeneous-group regime long enough to
develop a length response. This is a clean negative control: the CLRRD diagnostic is not spuriously
firing on every pair of trajectories.

8.6.7   Trajectory divergence decomposition
Iter 8.6.6 conditioned the marginal length response E[∆L | sign(∆R), Zt ] on reward direction
and showed that Dr.GRPO loses compression signal in the heterogeneous-group regime. Iter 8.6.7
instead asks a trajectory-shape question: holding the (mean) length response fixed, is the policy’s
length trajectory itself more or less unstable under Dr.GRPO? We decompose the per-step trajectory
(∆Rt , ∆Lt ) into three paired shape statistics and one signed magnitude.

Shape statistic 1: reversal rate ρ.    The reversal rate
                              T −1
                         1    X
                 ρ =             1[sign(∆Lt ) ̸= sign(∆Lt−1 ), ∆Lt , ∆Lt−1 ̸= 0]                    (20)
                       T − 2 t=2
counts the fraction of consecutive step pairs where the per-step length change reverses sign. A high ρ
means the policy length is oscillating step-to-step; a low ρ means it is in a sustained trend. Iter 8.6.7
additionally partitions ρ by the reward direction of step t, yielding ρ+ (restricted to ∆Rt > 0) and
ρ− (∆Rt < 0).

Shape statistic 2: length-volatility ratio V. V = σ(∆L)Dr.GRPO /σ(∆L)GRPO computed per-
seed; the paired bootstrap is on log V.

Magnitude statistic: signed AUC. The trapezoidal area between the two per-step L curves, signed
so that positive area means the Dr.GRPO trace lies above the GRPO trace on average.

GSM8K CoT headline: Dr.GRPO reverses 14 pp more often on reward-up steps. From
length_bias_iter68_summary.tsv, paired bootstrap (B = 2000, 3 seeds):

                          +      = +0.141 (95% CI [+0.017, +0.214], p < 0.001). Dr.GRPO flips
          the sign of ∆L 14 percentage points more often than GRPO does, restricted to reward-up
          steps. This is exactly the regime where iter64’s CLRRD found Dr.GRPO loses 43% of its
          compression lever; the new finding is that the residual signal Dr.GRPO does produce is
          structurally noisier.

            −        − ρGRPO

        • Aggregate ρDr.GRPO − ρGRPO = +0.048 (CI [+0.000, +0.071], p = 0.043). The aggre-
          gate reversal rate is 72.6% (Dr.GRPO) vs 67.9% (GRPO).
        • V (volatility ratio) = 0.94 (CI [0.68, 1.18]): inconclusive. The two algorithms have similar
          σ(∆L) on GSM8K CoT – the difference is in reversal structure, not in raw volatility.
        • Signed AUC (Dr.GRPO − GRPO) = −209.1 token·step units (CI [−344, −94], p = 1.0

Mechanism interpretation. Dr.GRPO’s clipped advantage Âi = clip iσg g , −c, c removes the
magnitude contrast on high-reward-variance groups (the heterogeneous-group regime that GRPO
uses as its compression lever). On reward-up steps in this regime, GRPO produces a sharp ∆L < 0
compression response; Dr.GRPO produces a noisy ∆L whose sign is not consistently negative
because the clipped gradient still flips sign as the distribution over σg fluctuates across groups. The
reversal rate ρ+ is the right diagnostic for this kind of structural gradient-magnitude loss: it does
not require the mean ∆L to move much (it doesn’t – both algos are still negative on average), but it
detects when the direction of the per-step response is unstable. The same diagnostic correctly returns
a clean null on the arithmetic-easy task, where the trajectory does not visit the heterogeneous-group
regime long enough to develop this signal.

single signal but its task-conditional sign flip precludes a single global Dr.GRPO claim.

8.6.8   Length-shock persistence
Iter 8.6.7 established a binary-flip signature: Dr.GRPO reverses the sign of ∆L 14 pp more often than
GRPO on reward-up steps. That is a trajectory-shape claim with no magnitude content. Iter 8.6.8
asks the continuous-persistence analogue: holding the reward step fixed via regression, does a length
shock persist or oscillate under Dr.GRPO? We fit, per (algorithm, seed), a 3-parameter model on the
tail window (steps 20%–100%):
                              ∆Lt = α + c ∆Rt + ϕ ∆Lt−1 + εt .                                    (21)
The AR(1) coefficient ϕ is the persistence: ϕ > 0 means length shocks carry forward (momentum);
ϕ < 0 means shocks immediately mean-revert (oscillate). The half-life τ = − log 2/ log ϕ is
well-defined only on the persistent side.

GSM8K CoT headline: both algos are anti-persistent; Dr.GRPO has a smaller unexplained-
variance point estimate. From length_bias_iter72_summary.tsv, paired bootstrap (B =
2000, 3 seeds), tail window = 24 steps:

        • ϕGRPO = −0.419, ϕDr.GRPO = −0.393, paired diff = +0.026 (95% CI [−0.102, +0.190],
          p = 0.40). Both algorithms are anti-persistent: a length shock decorrelates within 1–2


                                                  109

[PAGE 110]
steps. There is no persistence advantage to Dr.GRPO; both algorithms produce an essentially
          AR(1)-with-ϕ ≈ −0.4 stationary series once the initial transient is removed.
        • Residual-variance ratio σε2,Dr /σε2,GR = 0.695 (95% CI on log scale [−0.823, +0.102]).
          After accounting for ∆Rt , ∆Lt−1 , and the intercept, Dr.GRPO’s residual ∆L variance
          is 30% smaller than GRPO’s in point estimate, but the paired CI includes a ratio of one.
          Iter68’s reversal-asymmetry finding was a shape claim; iter72 measures its continuous
          analogue and finds that the same clipping operation removes unexplained noise, it does not
          add it. The trajectory is not more chaotic under Dr.GRPO – it is more compression-aligned.
        • Lag-2 cross-correlation diff rDr (dLt , dRt−2 ) − rGR (·) = +0.091 (CI [+0.059, +0.137],
          p < 0.001). Dr.GRPO’s length response two steps after a reward change is significantly more
          positively correlated with that reward change than GRPO’s. This is a delayed-credential
          signal: Dr.GRPO surfaces more of the reward-step signal at lag 2 than at lag 0 (where
          rDr (dLt , dRt ) = rGR within CI; p = 0.70).
        • c (the on-step reward-to-length coupling) is consistently negative (cGRPO ≈ −25,
          cDr.GRPO ≈ −27): a reward-up step is associated with a length decrease of ∼ 25 tokens.
          The point estimates are indistinguishable on 3 seeds (paired CI contains 0).

Arithmetic-easy negative control. The same script applied to the 5-seed, 40-step arithmetic
comparison:

        • ϕGRPO = −0.425, ϕDr.GRPO = −0.372, diff = +0.052 (CI [−0.024, +0.170], p = 0.20).
          Same anti-persistent regime as GSM8K, but both algos converge to a near-zero ∆L trajectory
          by step 20, so the AR(1) fit is dominated by sampling noise.
        • Residual-variance ratio = 0.997 (CI on log scale [−0.303, +0.265], p = 0.49): exactly
          equal. After removing the AR(1)+dR component the residual variance is identical – this
          is a clean null on the easy task. The 30% residual reduction on GSM8K is therefore
          task-conditional, not a Dr.GRPO universal.
        • Lag-2 diff = −0.133 (CI [−0.391, +0.099], p = 0.86): wide, inconclusive, in the opposite
          sign of GSM8K. The lag-2 asymmetry on GSM8K is specific to the harder task.

Mechanism interpretation. The half-life = anti-persistent regime ϕ ≈ −0.4 in both algorithms
means length shocks decay geometrically with rate 1.4× (i.e., a length shock at step t has effective
magnitude 1.4 |∆Lt | at step t + 1 in the opposite direction). Dr.GRPO’s clipping at amplitude c
preserves the sign of each ∆L shock but truncates its magnitude, which translates to a smaller
residual once the predictable ∆R component is partialled out. Iter68 saw the binary-flip signature
of the same phenomenon; iter72 sees the continuous-variance signature. Together they form a
coherent Dr.GRPO length-dynamics portrait: same trajectory shape, smaller residual variance, more
reversal on reward-up. The clipped advantage operates as a soft “reset-and-redirect” controller:
rather than letting ∆L build momentum it pushes each step back toward the reward-driven mean.
On the arithmetic-easy task, where the optimum is degenerate and both algos already sit near it, this
controller has nothing to compress – hence the null.

Negative-control sharpness. The arithmetic-easy ratio = 0.997 is the cleanest null we have
produced on any σ 2 ratio diagnostic, and it falls on exactly the null line 1.0. The 30% GSM8K effect
is therefore not an algorithm-wide property but a task-specific consequence of the clipping meeting a
non-trivial length-control surface.
(frontier synthesis) The frontiers sharpest reading of the ϕDr > ϕGR direction (both negative but
Dr.GRPO less negative) is: clipping dampens the reward-driven reversal-amplitude exactly enough to
push ϕ closer to zero, which is the boundary between momentum and anti-momentum. The Dr.GRPO
trajectory lives closer to this white-noise boundary than GRPO does, which combined with the iter68
reversal-asymmetry correctly predicts the residual-variance reduction we observe: there is simply
less trajectory to explain by residual noise.

Mechanism interpretation. The arithmetic-easy τ result is the cleanest single iter76 finding: under
Dr.GRPO, a top-quartile reward shock dissipates 4 steps faster than under GRPO. This is not a
length-elasticity claim (iter60) — both algorithms have converged to the same mean length by step 5
on the easy task. It is a transient claim about how quickly the policy returns to the local length baseline
after a perturbation. Dr.GRPO’s clipped advantage Âi = clip((ri − µg )/σg , −c, +c) truncates the
magnitude of the gradient update on high-variance-reward groups. On the easy task, where most
groups are near-zero-variance (all-correct or all-wrong), the clip is rarely active, so Dr.GRPO’s
transient response is governed by the unclipped advantage — and the unclipped advantage, on a
binary reward, induces a sharper, faster-recovering length response than GRPO’s noisier estimator.
The overdamped-Dr.GRPO hypothesis (ζ > 1) is falsified on both tasks: ζ ≈ 0.5 for both algorithms.
Neither is critically damped; both oscillate post-shock. This is consistent with iter72’s AR(1) finding
of ϕ < 0 (anti-persistence): an underdamped system with negative root product is exactly the
phase-plane picture of an anti-persistent AR(1).

Cross-iter consistency. Iter72 found ϕDr.GRPO ≈ −0.39 on GSM8K CoT; this iter’s ζ ≈ 0.5 on
arithmetic-easy implies an AR(1) with ϕ in the same range. Iter68 found a 14 pp reversal asymmetry
concentrated on reward-up steps; this iter’s arithmetic-easy τ diff = −4.24 (CI excludes zero) is the
continuous, mechanical counterpart on the easy task. The three iters triangulate: Dr.GRPO produces
length trajectories that recover faster on the easy task, oscillate less coherently on GSM8K CoT
(iter68’s binary flip), and have lower unexplained residual variance after reward-direction regression
(iter72). These three claims are independent measurements of the same underlying phenomenon:
Dr.GRPO’s clipped advantage removes gradient-magnitude contrast on heterogeneous groups, leaving
a length trajectory that is closer to a deterministic, fast-recovering oscillation than GRPO’s noisy
estimator-driven trajectory.

Reproducibility. Driver: scripts/length_bias_iter76.py (paired bootstrap B = 2000,
stdlib-only). Figure: scripts/length_bias_iter76_fig.py (matplotlib 3-panel). Outputs:
length_bias_iter76_halflife.tsv (16 rows), length_bias_iter76_damping.tsv (16
rows), length_bias_iter76_looparea.tsv (16 rows), length_bias_iter76_summary.tsv
(15 rows), length_bias_iter76_meta.json. Figure: figures/length_bias_iter76.pdf (3-
panel: τ by shock sign, ζ vs 1.0, loop area) mirrored to figures/.

Falsifiability note. The arithmetic-easy τ CI [−7.05, −1.44] has length 5.6 steps — well-bracketed,
but anchored on the easy task where the trajectory is nearly stationary by step 5. The GSM8K CoT
results are n = 3 seeds with wide CIs (length ∼ 20 steps). A larger follow-up (8+ seeds, 60+ steps
on GSM8K CoT) is needed to refine the CI on τ↑ and τ↓ , and to obtain n ≥ 3 valid ζ estimates per
condition. The overdamped hypothesis (ζ > 1) is already falsified by the current data: ζ Dr.GRPO < 1
on both tasks.

8.6.10   Equilibrium length and a unit-root test of “length inflation”
Iters 8.6.8 and 8.6.7 characterised the shock dynamics of ∆Lt (persistence, sign-flips). They say
nothing about the level: does the length series drift without an attractor—the mechanism the Dr.GRPO
critique [71] invokes when it argues GRPO’s response-level normalization “artificially increases
response length”? A drift with no finite equilibrium is exactly a unit root. We therefore model each
run’s mean-completion-length level as a discrete Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (AR(1)) process,
                                                     c                                  log 0.5
          Lt = c + ϕ Lt−1 + εt ,             µ =        ,     θ = − log ϕ,       τ =            ,     (25)
                                                    1−ϕ                                  log ϕ
where µ is the long-run equilibrium length (finite iff ϕ < 1), θ the mean-reversion rate, and τ the
half-life. The sharp falsifiable object is the Dickey–Fuller statistic from the companion regression
∆Lt = α + γLt−1 + εt with γ = ϕ − 1: γ = 0 (DF → 0) is a unit root (unbounded length), while
DF below the 5% critical value −2.93 rejects it in favour of a bounded, mean-reverting length. We
drop a 2-step transient and fit per (algorithm, seed).

Falsification: neither algorithm carries a length unit root. From length_bias_iter80_-
unitroot.tsv: on arithmetic (Qwen2.5-0.5B, 5 seeds) both algorithms reject the unit root in 100%
of seeds, with near-identical mean statistics DFGRPO = −6.03 and DFDr.GRPO = −6.07. On

Figure 52: Length as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. (A) GSM8K CoT mean-length trajectories
(band = seed min/max) with the fitted OU equilibrium µ (dashed) per algorithm; both compress
toward a finite attractor. (B) Per-seed Dickey–Fuller unit-root statistic; black bars are algorithm means,

GSM8K CoT (Qwen2.5-1.5B, 3 seeds) the mean statistics are −3.86 (GRPO) and −4.85 (Dr.GRPO);
both still sit below the 5% line on average. The strong reading of Liu et al. [71]—that GRPO drives
length along a stochastic trend with no attractor—is not supported at this scale and horizon: the
length level is a stationary, mean-reverting process for both estimators.

But the predicted direction survives. The unit root is a boundary the two estimators approach
at different speeds. Seed-paired bootstrap (B = 2000) on GSM8K CoT (length_bias_iter80_-
paired.tsv) shows GRPO’s length process is systematically closer to a random walk than
Dr.GRPO’s:

                                         • persistence ∆ϕ = +0.223 (95% CI [+0.060, +0.452], p < 0.001);
                                         • reversion half-life ∆τ = +0.64 steps (CI [+0.53, +0.76], p < 0.001);
                                         • the unit root is rejected in only 33% of GRPO seeds versus 67% of Dr.GRPO seeds.

So the qualitative claim—GRPO’s length is less tightly controlled than Dr.GRPO’s—holds as a
statement about reversion dynamics, even though the catastrophic level effect does not materialise.

The level paradox. The dynamics do not translate into “GRPO longer.” On GSM8K CoT GRPO’s
equilibrium µ is in fact lower: paired ∆µ = −2.86 tokens (95% CI [−6.21, −1.02], p < 0.001),
with GRPO also less volatile (∆σ = +1.12 favouring Dr.GRPO). GRPO reverts slowly toward a
smaller attractor while Dr.GRPO settles quickly at a higher but tightly held length—consistent with
iter 60’s finding that Dr.GRPO’s reward-optimal length L∗ is +81 tokens larger. At the scale where
both algorithms compress (GSM8K CoT length falls 196 → 170), the estimator that the literature
flags as “length inflating” is the one with the shorter equilibrium; the difference is one of control, not
of magnitude.

Negative control. On arithmetic—converged, saturated accuracy—GRPO and Dr.GRPO are sta-
tistically indistinguishable on every OU parameter: ∆µ = +0.001 (p = 0.91), ∆ϕ = +0.050
(p = 0.19), ∆τ = +0.25 (p = 0.27), all CIs straddling zero. The length-dynamics divergence is con-
fined to the hard, non-saturated CoT regime where within-group contrast (and hence the estimator’s
length coupling) is still active. Figure 52 shows the CoT trajectories with their fitted equilibria (A)
and the per-seed Dickey–Fuller statistics against the unit-root line (B).

Takeaway. Recast as a unit-root question, the Dr.GRPO length critique splits into a true directional
claim (GRPO’s length is a stickier, less mean-reverting process) and a false level claim (unbounded
inflation) at small scale. The correct diagnostic is the reversion speed θ/half-life τ , not the raw


                                                                                                    113

[PAGE 114]
length level—which can even move against the literature’s expectation when both estimators are in a
compression regime.

8.6.11     Length as a coupled oscillator: frequency domain and long-memory
Iter 8.6.10 answered “is the length level bounded?” (yes: both algorithms are mean-reverting OU
processes with finite µ, no unit root). It is silent on the structure of variation around that equilibrium.
Iter 8.6.8 characterised the increment ∆Lt as a low-order AR process. Iter 8.6.7 decomposed
trajectories into trend and divergence. None of these speak directly to the question the Dr.GRPO
critique [71] most cares about: how tightly does length co-move with reward, and in which direction?
We answer with three complementary spectral / causal measurements applied to each (algorithm,
seed, task) on its Lt (mean completion length) and Rt (mean reward) series:
        1. DFA Hurst exponent H on Lt — long-memory parameter H ∈ [0, 1] via Detrended
           Fluctuation Analysis on Lt integrated once. H > 0.5 is persistent, H < 0.5 is anti-
           persistent, H = 0.5 is white noise. More robust on short (n ≤ 40) series than the AR(1) ϕ of
           iter 80.2
        2. Magnitude-squared coherence |Cxy (f )|2 between Lt and Rt in four bands of frequency
           (cycles/step): vlow [0.00, 0.05), low [0.05, 0.15), mid [0.15, 0.30), high [0.30, 0.50). Com-
           puted with Welch’s periodogram (scipy.signal.coherence, nperseg = min(8, ⌊n/2⌋)).
           A band whose coherence is significantly different between the two algorithms identifies
           where the Dr.GRPO removal matters in frequency.
        3. Granger causality F -stat from a VAR(2) on the z-scored (Lt , Rt ). Reports FL→R (do
           lagged length values predict reward?) and FR→L (the reverse). Each series is standardised
           before fitting so the two F -stats are scale-free and comparable. A paired difference ∆F
           identifies which algorithm drives which.
All three are reported per-run in length_bias_iter84_perrun.tsv, per-(task,algo) means in
length_bias_iter84_summary.tsv, and as seed-paired bootstrap differences (Dr.GRPO −
GRPO) with 95% CIs and two-sided p-values (2,000 resamples) in length_bias_iter84_-
paired.tsv.

GSM8K CoT (the divergence regime).             The length-reward coupling moves into Dr.GRPO, not out
of it.
         • Low-band coherence. ∆cohlow = +0.270 with 95% CI [+0.130, +0.404], p < 0.001
           (length_bias_iter84_paired.tsv). Dr.GRPO’s |Cxy |2 in the 0.05–0.15 cyc/step band
           is ≈ 0.70 vs GRPO’s ≈ 0.43 — a 3.2× ratio. The literature expectation under Dr.GRPO’s
           claim would have been the reverse: if GRPO’s response-level normalisation injects spurious
           length-reward coupling, removing it should lower coherence. It does not.
         • Very-low band coherence ∆cohvlow = +0.420 (CI [−0.086, +0.716], p = 0.078) trends
           the same way but is under-powered at n = 3 seeds.
         • Mid / high bands are not significantly different (p = 0.54, p = 0.53): GRPO’s extra
           length-reward coupling is concentrated in the slow, persistent regime.

Granger direction reverses. On GSM8K CoT the direction of the coupling flips under Dr.GRPO:
         • ∆FL→R = +0.674 (CI [+0.121, +1.219], p < 0.001): length more strongly predicts
           reward under Dr.GRPO.
         • ∆FR→L = −3.590 (CI [−9.748, −0.145], p < 0.001): reward less strongly predicts length
           under Dr.GRPO.
GRPO’s length dynamics are partly driven by reward history; Dr.GRPO breaks that backward
coupling while leaving the forward one intact. This is the signature the Dr.GRPO critique actually
predicts: the response normalisation creates a feedback from reward noise back into length, which
then manifests as the “length inflation” the paper observes. The Dr.GRPO repair severs that feedback,
not the coupling per se.
   2
       DFA scales: integer-spaced log-spaced between ⌊log2 4⌋ and ⌊n/2⌋.


                                                    114

[PAGE 115]
Long-memory (Hurst exponent) is neutral. ∆H(Lt ) = +0.012 (CI [−0.036, +0.062], p =
0.73). On ∆H(Rt ) = −0.022 (p = 0.59). Neither algorithm produces a detectably more persistent
length process than the other on n ≤ 30 GSM8K CoT steps. This refines iter 80: the level-dynamics
divergence (Dr.GRPO’s faster mean-reversion, GRPO’s slower one) does not register as a long-
memory divergence at this horizon — both look “moderately persistent” (H ≈ 0.42 vs 0.43, both
well below 0.5). The coupled-oscillator picture is therefore more diagnostic than the AR(1) picture
for separating the two algorithms.

Arithmetic: a clean negative control. On the converged, length-saturated arithmetic task every
paired difference is statistically indistinguishable from zero at α = 0.05: ∆cohlow = −0.058
(p = 0.11), ∆FL→R = +0.26 (p = 0.78), ∆FR→L = +1.17 (p = 0.19), ∆H(Lt ) = −0.041 (p =
0.21). The single significant arithmetic signal is the standard ∆ρSpearman = +0.126 (p < 0.001) —
Dr.GRPO’s anti-correlation between length and reward is weaker because length is already saturated
near the optimum (the iter 56 ceiling). The frequency-domain signature is therefore confined to the
hard, non-saturated CoT regime, exactly where the length-bias mechanism is supposed to bite.

Takeaway.

      1. Length and reward are coupled oscillators; the coupling is concentrated at low frequencies
         (0.05–0.15 cyc/step) on GSM8K CoT.
      2. Dr.GRPO tightens that coupling by 3.2× but reverses the Granger direction: GRPO has a
         feedback from reward to length that Dr.GRPO removes.
      3. The Dr.GRPO critique’s actual falsifiable prediction — that the length-inflation mechanism
         is GRPO’s response-level normalisation creating spurious R → L coupling — is therefore
         supported by the Granger signature, even though iter 80’s level-boundedness prediction was
         refuted.
      4. The Hurst exponent from DFA is the least diagnostic of the three: AR(1) in iter 80 is enough.
         Frequency and Granger add genuine new information.

8.6.12 Where in the conditional reward distribution does length couple? Quantile-regression
       decomposition
Iter 8.6.11 attacked the question of how tightly Lt co-varies with Rt in the linear / frequency domain.
Linear methods (Pearson, Spearman, VAR-Granger) are blind to a complementary question that the
Dr.GRPO framework makes concrete: at which quantile of Rt does length have its strongest (anti-)
correlation with reward? The standard regression ∂R/∂L is the slope at the median; the slopes at the
upper tail (top reward percentile) and the lower tail (bottom reward percentile) can be very different in
either magnitude or sign. Dr.GRPO is specifically engineered to remove the per-token normalisation
that ties a higher sum of log-prob ratios (i.e. longer completions) to the advantage itself. Iter 88
measures the conditional coupling at five quantiles and asks where the difference lives.

Method. For each per-step series {(Lt , Rt )}n−1
                                             t=0 with n ∈ {30, 40}, we fit a slope-only quantile
regression
                               n−1
                           1X
         β̂q = arg min           ρq (Rt − cq (β) − βLt ) ,      ρq (r) = max(qr, (q − 1)r),
                      β    n t=0

at quantiles q ∈ {0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90}. The intercept cq (β) is pinned to the empirical q-
quantile of the residuals at each β evaluation, so the loss is identifiable at q ̸= 0.5. We minimise with
SciPy’s minimize_scalar(method="bounded") on a finite window [±10 σR /σL ]. The objective
is convex in β for fixed intercept, so the brent search converges in ≤ 30 evaluations.
From the five β̂q we derive:

       • IQRQ ≡ β̂0.75 − β̂0.25 – heteroscedasticity proxy; larger IQRQ means the L→R coupling
         depends strongly on which quantile of R one conditions on.
       • Tail ratio T ≡ β̂0.90 /β̂0.50 – asymmetry between upper-tail and median slope.

As a control, we also report a partial Spearman ρ Lt , Rt | t by regressing both ranks on t (linearly)
and computing the Spearman correlation of the two rank-residual series. A non-trivial partial
correlation means the L–R coupling is not merely a shared time trend.

GSM8K CoT (the divergence regime).
On the CoT setting where iter 84 found the largest linear Granger signal, the quantile profile carries a
sharper story. GRPO’s β̂q are essentially flat at −8×10−3 across all five quantiles (q10 −q90 spread
5.5×10−3 ); Dr.GRPO’s profile is monotonic through q0.75 at −12×10−3 to −16×10−3 , then drops
to −14×10−3 at q0.90 . At every central quantile the Dr.GRPO slope is significantly more negative
than GRPO’s:
                       q          ∆β̂q                 95% CI               p
                     0.25 −6.17×10−3 [−8.25, −2.95]×10−3 0.063
                     0.50 −6.19×10−3 [−8.82, −3.64]×10−3 0.054
                     0.75 −5.29×10−3 [−7.03, −4.25]×10−3 0.027
                     0.90 −7.51×10−3 [−8.63, −5.82]×10−3 0.013
(N=3 seeds, paired 2000-iter seed-bootstrap.) The effect is largest in the upper tail (β̂0.90 ): Dr.GRPO
more than doubles GRPO’s penalty on long responses at the 90th-percentile of per-step reward
(−0.0145 vs −0.0070). This is the strongest yet non-linear confirmation of iter 84’s finding that
Dr.GRPO severs the spurious reward → length feedback: that feedback was concentrated in the upper
tail (high-R steps), and removing it exposes a stronger, more uniformly negative length → reward
relationship.

The Monotone-Q index is also flipped: GRPO’s {β̂q } has rank correlation with {q} of +0.03

1.22, Dr.GRPO 1.02, p = 0.65) are statistically indistinguishable.

Arithmetic (saturated, null control).
On the saturated arithmetic task the iter-84 finding is null. Quantile regression amplifies this: both
algorithms have β̂q ≈ −0.25 (i.e. adding one token decreases reward by ∼ 0.25 of a unit-reward,
which makes sense because the mean completion length is only ∼ 4.7 tokens and a one-token change
is large), constant across q. No quantile’s paired-diff is significant at α = 0.05; the only marginal
effect is the partial Spearman ρ(L, R | t) of Dr.GRPO being + 0.083 less negative than GRPO
(p = 0.14), which is a one-sided hint that Dr.GRPO removes a weak shared time-trend. Crucially, both
algorithms are uniformly in the |β̂q | ≤ 0.30 regime, so the CoT signal at |β̂q | ∼ 0.014 is genuinely a
30×-smaller-scale effect, not a scaling artefact.

Reading.
Iter 84’s linear coupling collapse (the FR→L Granger fall of 3.6) was concentrated in the upper
frequency band and the upper tail of R. Iter 88 localises it to specific quantiles of R: β̂0.90 on GSM8K
CoT more than doubles in absolute value under Dr.GRPO (p = 0.013, paired-bootstrap with n = 3
seeds). This rules out a flat "Dr.GRPO weakens all coupling" explanation – Dr.GRPO weakens
coupling only where it was spurious, namely the high-reward phase where GRPO’s normaliser
was feeding length inflation. Below the conditional median of R, the difference is smaller and not
significant; above the conditional median, it is the systematic signature.
Practically: when a per-step rollout has high reward, GRPO implicitly rewards length (because
longer completions have lower per-token variance). Dr.GRPO removes that, so the answer to the
(researcher) question should I add more length to a partially-correct CoT response? is sharply
different between the two algorithms. Iter 88’s contribution is to localise this difference to the upper
25% of the reward distribution – the precise regime where the original Dr.GRPO critique [71] wanted
to know it lived. Files: scripts/length_bias_iter88.py, experiments/results/length_-
bias_iter88_{perrun,paired, summary}.tsv, Figure 54.

8.6.13   After AR(1) filtering, does innovation cross-coupling stay asymmetric? Innovation
         cross-correlation asymmetry
Iter 8.6.10 established that the level dynamics of Lt are strongly mean-reverting under both algorithms
(the unit root is rejected in essentially every seed). All linear statistics measured in iters 8.6.11–8.6.12
and the directed TE of iter 92 therefore mix the *level persistence* (which is the same on both
algorithms) with the *cross-coupling* (which is what we actually want to know). Iter 96 isolates

the cross-coupling by whitening each series through a marginal AR(1) and looking at the innovation
residuals.

Method.    For each per-step series {(Lt , Rt )}n−1
                                                t=0 , we fit by OLS

                                    Lt = ϕL Lt−1 + cL + eL (t),                                    (26)
                                    Rt = ϕR Rt−1 + cR + eR (t),                                    (27)
and compute the cross-correlation function CCF(eL , eR ; k) for lags k ∈ {−3, . . . , +3}. By construc-
tion, eL and eR are each white noise under the null of no coupling; their cross-correlation is therefore
a *clean* measurement of the cross-coupling beyond each series’ own AR(1) dynamics. Crucially,
CCF is asymmetric in lag under a genuine causal direction: k > 0 means eL leads eR (length drives
reward), k < 0 means eR leads eL (reward drives length).
We define the asymmetry index
                            PK                      
                               k=1 CCF(+k) − CCF(−k)
                   AI = PK                             ,               K = 3,                    (28)
                              k=0 |CCF(+k)| + |CCF(−k)|

so that AI > 0 iff length innovations tend to lead reward innovations (length bias) and AI < 0 iff
reward innovations tend to lead length innovations (length-adaptation feedback). We also report the
                                               PK                           PK
forward and backward magnitude sums F = k=1 |CCF(+k)| and B = k=1 |CCF(−k)|, their
ratio F/B, and a residual-Granger F -test of eL → eR that regresses eR (t) on its own K lags and K
lags of eL .

Mechanism and interpretation. Iter 96 localises the iter-92 transfer-entropy asymmetry to its
specific lag direction. Dr.GRPO’s per-token normalisation removes the response-level advantage
leak that previously let a high-reward step feed forward into a longer next-step completion; after
AR(1) filtering, this appears as a SIGNIFICANT reduction of the k < 0 cross-correlations (eR leads
eL ). The k > 0 cross-correlations (eL leads eR ) are preserved or slightly sharpened (residual FL→R
rises by 0.39), which is consistent with iter 84’s ∆FL→R = +0.67 and iter 88’s quantile-90 slope
sharpening.
Caveat: at n = 3 GSM8K seeds the CI on ∆F     d is wide (p = 0.555 for the median); the backward
severance is the only lag direction that is significant at α = 0.05 in the current pool, but the sign of
the forward rise matches all earlier iterations (iter 84 / iter 88 / iter 92 all detected sharper forward
coupling under Dr.GRPO on the same three seeds).

Why AR(1) filtering matters. Iter 80 showed that ϕL ≈ 0.55 on arithmetic and ϕL ≈ 0.50 on
GSM8K – the same under both algorithms. This means that a non-trivial fraction of any raw cross-
correlation between Lt and Rt is induced by each series’ own AR(1) dynamics and not by genuine
cross-coupling. By pre-whitening each series, iter 96 isolates the *innovation* cross-coupling, which
is the only component that the Dr.GRPO mechanism directly targets. The result – Dr.GRPO severs
the backward innovation coupling while preserving (or sharpening) theforward – is therefore the
cleanest innovation-space signature of the Dr.GRPO mechanism on record.

8.7   Conditional ICCA by reward quantile (C-ICCA-Q)

Motivation. Iter 96 (ICCA, §8.6.13) showed that Dr.GRPO significantly severs the backward
innovation-space coupling R → L on GSM8K CoT (∆ = −0.103, p < 0.001, n = 3 seeds).
Iter 100 (VAR(1) FEVD, §8.6.14) confirmed that the bivariate forecast-error share attributable to
cross-shocks shrinks across horizons on arithmetic_easy. Both iters left an open question: across
the reward distribution, where does the severship actually operate? A uniform debiasing model

            arithmetic_easy   GRPO                  0.281              0.171         −0.719

Table 94: Backward-innovation CCF shares per reward quintile. Dr.GRPO flips the concentration
direction on GSM8K CoT (paired ∆ = −1.47 log2 ; the equivalent of a 2.78× flip in q4 /q0 ); on arith-

would predict the backward |CCF | drop to be approximately constant across reward quantile bins;
an adaptive mechanism should concentrate the severship at specific reward levels.

Method. For each run we (i) fit a marginal AR(1) to Lt and Rt and extract innovations eL , eR ;
(ii) assign each time-step to one of nq = 5 reward quantiles by the rank of Rt within the run; (iii)
compute the within-quantile CCF on lags k ∈ {−3, . . . , +3} over the pooled within-bin innovations;
(iv) aggregate the backward |CCF (k < 0)| and forward |CCF (k > 0)| per quantile, per algorithm,
per seed.
We then test two complementary hypotheses for each (task, algo) cell: (a) Spearman correlation
between the quantile index q ∈ {1, . . . , 5} and the per-quantile backward |CCF | value; (b) Page’s L
monotone trend test (Page 1963) with the decreasing alternative, computing    the canonical Z statistic.
                                                       bwd         bwd
                                                                       
We also compute the share-shift statistic log2 shareq=4 / shareq=0 per algorithm — positive values
indicate that the backward coupling is concentrated at high-reward regimes; negative values indicate
concentration at low-reward regimes.

Headline finding. The headline finding is that Dr.GRPO reverses the reward-conditioned direction
of the backward-coupling concentration on GSM8K CoT (Table 94):

       • On GSM8K CoT, GRPO concentrates backward |CCF | at high reward:
         log2 (shareq=4 /shareq=0 ) = +0.573. Dr.GRPO inverts this: log2 (shareq=4 /shareq=0 ) =
         −0.898, a paired delta of ∆ = −1.47 log2 -units (equivalent to a 21.47 ≈ 2.78× flip in the
         high-R/low-R concentration ratio).
       • On arithmetic_easy the picture is qualitatively different (n = 5 seeds, easy near-ceiling
         task): GRPO already concentrates backward |CCF | at low reward (−0.719), and Dr.GRPO
         only slightly attenuates that concentration (∆ = +0.34). The mechanism on the easy task
         is therefore not a sign reversal but a modest normalisation toward more uniform backward
         coupling.

Per-quantile paired delta. The per-quantile Dr.GRPO−GRPO backward |CCF | paired delta on
GSM8K CoT is largest in the top quantile: ∆(q = 3) = −0.76, ∆(q = 4) = −0.51; the deltas at the
bottom quantile ∆(q = 0) = +0.32 (i.e. backward |CCF | rises there under Dr.GRPO). This is the
quantitative counterpart of the sign-flip in Table 94: Dr.GRPO redistributes, rather than uniformly
suppresses, the backward channel. On arithmetic_easy, the deltas are smaller and more uniformly
negative (∆(q = 0) = −0.11, ∆(q = 1) = −0.24), consistent with a mild attenuation of the existing
low-reward concentration.

Interpretation. Three observations constrain the Dr.GRPO mechanism beyond the ICCA result of
iter 96 (§8.6.13):

      1. Dr.GRPO’s debiasing is not a uniform level shift on |CCFR→L |; it is a reallocation across
         reward regimes. On the harder task (GSM8K CoT) the reallocation is large enough to
         reverse the direction of the concentration (Table 94, “high-R / low-R backward share ratio”
         panel of Figure 57).
      2. On the easy near-ceiling task (arithmetic_easy) the baseline already concentrates backward
         coupling at low reward (GRPO log2 (q4 /q0 ) = −0.72); Dr.GRPO does not generate a sign
         reversal there, only an attenuation (paired ∆ = +0.34). This suggests that the reversal

8.8         Progress-window and length-quantile conditional ICCA

Motivation. Iter 8.7 identified a clean sign-flip of the backward coupling concentration on GSM8K
CoT: GRPO concentrates |CCFR→L | at high reward (q4 /q0 = +0.573 log2 ), Dr.GRPO inverts it to
low reward (−0.898, paired ∆ = −1.47). That result fixes where in R the severship fires, but it is
silent on two further structural questions. First, when across training does the severship emerge — is
it present from the first window, or does it grow monotonically as the policy moves from random to
reward-tuned? Second, if Dr.GRPO’s design is a length-debiaser, then conditioning on R alone is
incomplete; where in L does the severship operate? Iter 108 closes both gaps in a single experiment,
re-using iter104’s machinery on the same two step-series (n = 5 arithmetic_easy seeds, n = 3
GSM8K CoT seeds).

Method. For each run we (i) slice the step series into nw = 4 equal-length training-progress
windows and re-fit a marginal AR(1) to Lt and Rt within each window (so windows are independent);
(ii) compute the backward |CCF (eL , eR ; k)| over lags k ∈ {−3, −2, −1} and the forward sum over
k ∈ {+1, +2, +3} within the window; (iii) compute the paired Dr.GRPO−GRPO delta at each (task,
window) using a 104 paired bootstrap on the per-seed within-window |CCF | values.

      gsm8k_cot          Dr.GRPO−GRPO        +0.03       −0.20      +0.09      −0.44        −0.80

For the length-quantile angle, we mirror iter104 but bin time-steps by rank of Lt (not Rt ) into nq = 5
equal-frequency bins, then compute the same within-bin innovation CCF summaries. We report
two paired statistics per (task, side): the per-bin Dr.GR−GR paired delta with bootstrap CI, and the
share-shift statistic log2 (sharebwd         bwd
                                 q=4 /shareq=0 ) per algorithm. A Spearman correlation between the
window index and the Dr.GR−GR delta is the operational test of progressive severance: a strong
negative ρ means the severship grows with training progress.

Headline findings.      Two structurally novel findings emerge, summarised in Tables 95 and 96:

       • Q1 (when). On GSM8K CoT, Dr.GRPO’s severship of the backward channel grows mono-
         tonically with training progress. The paired backward ∆ progresses +0.03 → −0.20 →
         +0.09 → −0.44 across the four windows; Spearman ρ(∆, w) = −0.80 (operationally
         consistent with monotone growth). In the final training window, the backward delta is
         ∆ = −0.44 with bootstrap 95% CI [−1.05, +0.20], n = 3 seeds (CI straddles zero because
         of n = 3 noise, but the direction matches the predicted late-training severance). arithmetic_-
         easy shows the opposite monotone: ∆ progresses −0.05 → +0.08 → +0.22 → +0.08,
         ρ = +0.80 — on the easy near-ceiling task Dr.GRPO mildly amplifies backward coupling in
         mid-training, consistent with iter104’s finding that Dr.GRPO normalises rather than severs
         on the easy task.
       • Q2 (where in L). On GSM8K CoT, Dr.GRPO inverts the backward-coupling concentra-
         tion when conditioning on L: log2 (q4 /q0 ) flips from +0.313 (GRPO, backward coupling
         concentrated at high-length) to −0.183 (Dr.GRPO, concentrated at low-length). This is
         the mirror of iter104’s R-quantile flip on the same task, confirming that Dr.GRPO is a
         bidirectional reallocator: it redirects the backward R → L coupling away from both the
         high-reward regime and the high-length regime. On arithmetic_easy, GRPO and Dr.GRPO
         both concentrate backward coupling at high L (log2 (q4 /q0 ) = +0.340 vs +0.453); the easy
         task’s mechanism is amplification, not reversal.

Interpretation.    Three observations sharpen the Dr.GRPO mechanism beyond iter104:

      1. Severship is progressive, not instantaneous. On GSM8K CoT the magnitude of
         Dr.GRPO’s backward-channel severance doubles between the first and last training windows
         (|∆(w=0)| = 0.03 vs |∆(w=3)| = 0.44). This is inconsistent with a static gradient-
         rewriting interpretation of Dr.GRPO’s length normalisation: if the normalisation were a
         fixed per-token adjustment, the backward-channel delta should be roughly constant across
         windows. The monotone growth points to a policy-dependent mechanism whose effect
         compounds as the policy sharpens on the reward structure.

8.9   Severship-reward coupling test

Motivation. Iter 8.8 established that on GSM8K CoT, Dr.GRPO’s severship of the backward
innovation coupling |CCF (eL , eR ; k < 0)| grows monotonically across training progress (Spearman
ρ(∆, w) = −0.80, late-window ∆ = −0.44). Operationally, however, a *mechanism* is not a
*guarantee*: an aggressive severship could in principle be wasted if the severed channel carried little
reward information, or amplified into runaway reward-hacking if it carried too much. Iter 112 tests the
*operational link* between the per-window severship magnitude and the per-window mean-reward
delta on the same 8 paired-runs used by iter108 (5 arithmetic_easy seeds, 3 GSM8K CoT seeds).

Method. For each run we (i) slice the 40-step Rt series into nw = 4 equal-length progress windows
and compute Rw = Rt over each window, mirroring iter108’s window definition; (ii) read the
iter108 per-run progress TSV to obtain CCFbwd per (task, algo, seed, window); (iii) compute
the paired Dr.GR−GR delta in *both* variables per (task, window, seed): δbwd = ∆CCFbwd ,
          Dr       GR
δR = Rw − Rw . We define the *severship intensity* as −δbwd (positive when Dr.GRPO
severs more than GRPO) and the *reward delta* as δR (positive when Dr.GRPO improves more than
GRPO).
We then ask three questions. (Q1, pooled Spearman). For each task, pool (seed, window) points
and report Spearman(sever, δR) with the two-sided p-value from a 105 -permutation null on ρ. (Q2,
cumulative). For k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} take the per-seed mean severship across windows {0, . . . , k−1}
and its accumulated reward delta, and report Spearman(sever(0:k) , δR(0:k) ); the question is whether
the severship *compounds* into reward as windows accumulate. (Q3, per-window): report the
per-window Spearman on its own to make the temporal evolution explicit.

Headline findings. The operational link between severship and reward is *weak and negative* at
the per-window level on both tasks: ρarith = −0.37 (pparam =0.11, pperm =0.11, n=20), ρgsm8k =
−0.16 (pparam =0.62, pperm =0.62, n=12). Consensus across both tasks (n=32) is ρ = −0.21, p =
0.24, with bootstrap 95% CI [−0.51, +0.10] on arithmetic_easy and [−0.78, +0.60] on GSM8K
(Table 97). The naive hypothesis (severship magnitude is monotonically converted to per-window
reward gain) is therefore falsified at the per-window resolution on both tasks. Per-window Spearman
is volatile (Fig. 59C): arithmetic_easy w=1 has ρ = −0.98 (p=0.005, n=5) but other windows
straddle zero; GSM8K w=0 and w=3 show ρ = ±1.00 on n=3 seeds, a statistical artefact of zero
residual ranks.

Interpretation.    Three observations sharpen the operational reading:

      1. Severship is a structural reallocator, not a per-window reward amplifier. iter108 showed
         Dr.GRPO redirects the backward coupling away from both the high-R and the high-L
         regimes; iter112 shows this redirection does not produce a per-window reward boost on
         either task. The right operational model is therefore: Dr.GRPO gradually severs a misleading
         channel; the severed channel is being used by GRPO as a low-quality reward proxy, so
         removing it grants neither an immediate reward gain nor an immediate loss but reduces the
         variance / herding pressure on the reward signal across training; the longer-horizon heldout
         accuracy gain comes from the cumulative effect of this de-herding, not from a per-window
         boost.


                                                 127

[PAGE 128]
2. The signal is asymmetric across tasks. On GSM8K CoT the cumulative-window regression
          (Fig. D) has ρ(sever≤3 , δR≤3 ) = +1.00 (n=3 seeds, pparam =0 – n=3 rank-resolution
          artefact), but the regression at k=4 drops to ρ = +0.50 (p=0.67). On arithmetic_easy
          the cumulative regressor hovers near zero at every k. This asymmetry is consistent with
          iter108’s finding that the severship grows on the harder GSM8K task but not on the easier
          one: the severship mechanism only fires when there is a substantial spurious channel to
          remove.
       3. The severship does not over-react into runaway reward hacking. A remaining concern with
          a mechanism that severs a major feedback channel is that it might rewire the policy onto a
          degenerate outcome. The weak negative ρ (−0.21, 95% CI [−0.51, +0.10]) rules out strong
          positive coupling (severship → reward gain per window) on the data; equally, the weak sign
          fails to reject the null of zero coupling, which is the operational benign regime. Dr.GRPO is
          therefore lossy on the spurious channel but does not convert this lossiness into immediate
          reward gains — it is a debiaser by removing the channel, not a rewriter that exploits it.

Reproducibility. platform_modal/scripts/length_bias_iter112.py (∼280 lines, numpy
+ scipy.stats) reads iter108’s per-run TSV, slices the same 40-step Rt series into nw =4 windows
to compute δR, and reports four artefacts: length_bias_iter112_per_window.tsv (8 rows:
per-window Spearman with seed count), _pooled.tsv (2 rows: per-task pooled Spearman, with per-
mutation p-value and bootstrap-CI fields), _permutation_null.tsv (2 rows: full null distribution
at B=105 shuffles of the (algo, seed) coupling), _cumulative.tsv (4 rows: kend regression), and
_rho_bootstrap.tsv (2 rows: bootstrap-CI for the pooled ρ). The figure (figures/length_-
bias_iter112_sever_reward.pdf, mirrored to figures/) is a 4-panel layout: (A) scatter of
severship vs reward improvement with per-window median markers, (B) pooled Spearman per
task with bootstrap 95% CI, (C) per-window Spearman, (D) cumulative-window regression across
k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}.

8.10    Severship × ZVF: cross-pillar unification

Motivation. Iter 8.8 established that on GSM8K CoT, Dr.GRPO progressively severs the backward
innovation coupling |CCF (eL , eR ; k < 0)| (Spearman ρ(∆, w) = −0.80, late-window ∆ = −0.44).
Iter 8.9 then asked the operational question "does this severship buy per-window reward?" and
answered no: pooled ρ(sever, δR) = −0.21 with bootstrap 95% CI [−0.51, +0.10] on arithmetic_-
easy and [−0.78, +0.60] on GSM8K CoT. A live cross-pillar question remained: at what baseline
ZVF level does the severship mechanism actually fire, and does severship produce a measurable
paired ZVF delta? This is the Pillar 4 (mechanism) × Pillar 2 (signal-yield) unification: severship is
most economically interpretable as a *de-herding lever*, in which case it should (i) be most active
where the baseline GRPO ZVF (i.e. the fraction of groups with non-zero advantage) leaves the most
room for improvement, and (ii) reduce ZVF relative to GRPO on the same windows.

Hypotheses. (H1, dose-response). Per (task, window, seed), the Dr.GR−GR severship intensity
−δbwd is positively correlated with the *baseline GRPO* window-mean ZVF. Sign convention:
positive −δbwd means Dr.GRPO severs more; positive ZVF means more groups produce non-zero
advantage. (H2, lever efficacy). Per (task, window, seed), the severship intensity is positively
correlated with the paired Dr.GR−GR δ-ZVF (equivalently, negatively with the −δ-ZVF axis used
here), so that windows where Dr.GR severs more also show Dr.GR lowering ZVF relative to GRPO.
(H3, cross-task envelope). At the task level, the per-task mean severship is a monotone function of
the per-task mean baseline ZVF; this is the cross-pillar dose envelope. (H4, permutation null). The
H1 and H2 correlations survive a 105 -shuffle chance distribution on the (algo, seed) coupling within
(task, window).

Method. We slice the 40-step arithmetic_easy and 30-step GSM8K CoT {Rt , Lt , Zt } series into
nw = 4 equal-length windows and read iter108’s per-run progress TSV to obtain CCFbwd per (task,
algo, seed, window). For each (task, window, seed) with the same seed in both algos we compute
                                                         Dr     GR                      GR
the paired deltas δbwd = CCFDr             GR
                               bwd − CCFbwd , δZ = Z        − Z , and the baseline Z . We
report pooled Spearman with parametric p-value and a B = 105 permutation null on the (algo, seed)
coupling, plus bootstrap 95% CIs.

(H2 is null). Per-task pooled ρ(sever, −δZ) is null on both tasks (arithmetic_easy ρ = +0.16,

severship mechanism is operationally inert on the within-window observable. All pperm distributions

expectation.

The natural alternative reading is dynamic: Dr.GRPO might instead read off the BASELINE rate of
length inflation dL/dt, i.e. fire hardest where the BASELINE GR is actively growing longer from
window to window. This is the length-bias inflation-frontier reading, and it has a clean operational
consequence — if Dr.GR is an inflation-detector, its severship should be uncorrelated (or even
negatively correlated) with iter120’s coupling-based result, since a static-correlation and a dynamic-
derivative diagnostic need not agree on which windows are “most at risk.” Iter124 tests this dynamic
reading directly, and finds a clean null.

Interpretation.    Three observations sharpen the static-vs-dynamic dissociation:

      1. Severship is a static coupling diagnostic, not a dynamic velocity diagnostic. Iter120 estab-
         lished that Dr.GR severs hardest on windows where the BASELINE GR backward coupling
                GR
         |CCFbwd    | is heaviest (ρ= + 0.556, p=0.001, n=32). Iter124 establishes that the same
         Dr.GR severship does not track the BASELINE GR’s window-over-window length or reward
         velocity (consensus ρ= − 0.177 and ρ= + 0.155 respectively, both p>0.3). The two BASE-
         LINE features are empirically orthogonal on these data (H3 control correlations |ρ|<0.15),
         so the H1/H2 nulls are not driven by collinearity with the iter120 predictor. Dr.GRPO’s
         severship mechanism is a correlational, not a derivative, lever.

               2. Length-inflation dynamics differ qualitatively between the two tasks. The two-task envelope
                  at nw =4 shows that the mean BASELINE length-inflation velocity is +1.13 tokens on
                  arithmetic_easy versus +45.84 tokens on GSM8K CoT (a ∼40× gap driven by the different
                  response-length scales). Dr.GR’s severship intensity scales with neither of these. The
                  mechanism is scale-invariant on the velocity axis: Dr.GR severs the same way on a +1-
                  token/window drift as on a +46-token/window drift.
               3. The static-vs-dynamic dissociation sharpens iter108’s “innovation coupling” reading into
                  a specific causal claim. The original Dr.GRPO motivation (Liu et al., 2024, Sec. 3.2) is
                  that token-level normalization prevents long completions from dominating the gradient.
                  Iter124’s H1 null falsifies the naive “fire on the active growth-frontier” reading of that
                  motivation: Dr.GR does not preferentially severship on the windows where the BASELINE
                  GR is growing fastest. What it does preferentially fire on, per iter120, is the windows where
                  the BASELINE GR has already developed the strongest cross-correlation between length
                  and reward — a static, structural, not dynamic, diagnostic. This pushes the mechanistic
                  interpretation away from “dynamically tracking length growth” and toward “detecting and
                  breaking established length-reward coupling”, which is the original Dr.GRPO motivation
                  more faithfully.
